Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events, whereas the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term. In simulations, interval RRB responded to an omitted term's effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum over a null reference for chance imbalance was 3.5-6.0% (nominal 5%) when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and mostly 1.0-4.5% under censoring in a single interval. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero, whereas the end-of-grace SMD reached 0.40; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In a case study, interval RRB flagged a dispensing indicator outside the censoring model. Interval RRB checks the censoring model, and cumulative RRB the representation of the baseline population.
Methodology.comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables; Supporting Information (16 pages) as ancillary file. R package and reproduction code: https://github.com/Nonokyu/ccwbalance (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24013295)

Methodology.title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity
Methodology.summary: This paper develops a general M-estimation framework for censored regression models under endogeneity. A two-stage estimation is proposed to address the issue of endogeneity in the first stage and the issue of censoring in linear regression models in the second stage. The issue of endogeneity is addressed via instrumental variables using the control function approach. The issue of censoring in linear regression models is addressed via M-estimation using a suitably defined class of loss functions yielding a class of estimators. Thus, the proposed general M-estimation framework nests several existing estimators as special cases for the respective loss functions. Moreover, this provides flexibility of accommodating a broad range of robust loss functions that have not previously been studied in the context of censored regression. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the proposed class of estimators. An empirical study based on simulated datasets is conducted to illustrate general M-estimation for various choices of loss functions and to examine the finite-sample performance of various resulting estimators.

Methodology.title: Covariance-Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference
Methodology.summary: In prediction-powered inference, predictions supplement labeled outcomes to improve estimation. We combine a prediction-corrected score and an auxiliary moment in a generalized method of moments (GMM) criterion. The resulting estimator is first-order equivalent to the corresponding corrected-score root under regularity conditions, but the auxiliary penalty can change the finite-sample fit. In a multiparameter Gaussian linear model with low noise, retaining this penalty reduces risk relative to bounded scalar corrected-score roots. We then introduce covariance-calibrated prediction-powered inference (CC-PPI), which uses prediction scores from both samples to reweight the penalty. With a spectrally protected half-strength update, CC-PPI retains regular first-order efficiency and strictly reduces risk relative to uncalibrated full GMM in a Gaussian linear low-noise regime that tolerates some prediction error and in a structured multiparameter logistic model conditional on the existence of a finite pilot estimate. Targeted simulations isolate the gains from calibration and show that they can reverse as prediction error grows. Broader simulations and four applications evaluate point estimation and the coverage and width of full-refit bootstrap intervals for linear projections.

Methodology.title: Anchors Away: Navigating Single-Arm Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR-SA)
Methodology.summary:
Unanchored indirect treatment comparisons using single-arm evidence are increasingly used in health technology assessment (HTA) when anchored comparisons of randomized evidence are not possible. Existing population-adjusted methods, including matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) and simulated treatment comparison (STC), are generally limited to pairwise analyses and typically estimate marginal effects in the comparator study population, which may differ from the decision-relevant target population.
  We propose multilevel unanchored meta-regression for single-arm indirect comparisons (ML-UMR-SA), a Bayesian outcome-regression framework for synthesizing individual patient data and aggregate data from single-arm evidence. ML-UMR-SA respecifies multilevel network meta-regression to pool absolute outcomes rather than relative treatment effects, jointly modeling individual- and aggregate-level data and linking aggregate outcomes through marginalization over study-specific covariate distributions, enabling estimation across multiple treatments, studies, and target populations.
  ML-UMR-SA distinguishes assumptions required to identify treatment effects from those required to transport results to target populations. Valid inference relies on strong and often unverifiable assumptions, particularly conditional constancy of absolute effects and cross-treatment identifying assumptions such as the shared prognostic factor assumption (SPFA). These requirements are made explicit within a Bayesian modeling framework that facilitates sensitivity analyses.
  In simulations without unobserved confounding, ML-UMR-SA produced low bias and nominal coverage for comparator-population effects. Transportability to alternative populations depended critically on identifying assumptions, whereas incorporating subgroup information restored near-unbiased estimation and nominal coverage.

Methodology.title: Calibrated Order-Randomized Rosenblatt Tests
Methodology.summary: We test whether a multivariate vector X conforms to a specified distribution F, as in copula modelling and density forecasting. The Rosenblatt transform reduces this to testing uniformity, but its arbitrary coordinate ordering affects power under dependence. We study order randomization: transforming under many random orderings and merging evidence with dependence-robust rules. Reordering only redistributes the Mahalanobis signal energy, so one ordering is a lucky or unlucky draw, and pooling raises calibrated power. We compare against two order-invariant baselines, the chi-squared energy test and the symmetric-root test. With F known, the e-value average over orderings is at least as powerful as the symmetric-root test in every setting we ran, and as the chi-squared test on concentrated and fully diffuse departures. With Gaussian mean and covariance estimated, the classical conditional probability integral transform keeps each ordering's p-values exact and e-values valid, a parametric bootstrap calibrates the pooled tests, and the comparisons hold except for deficits of at most 0.02 against the symmetric-root test on single-coordinate departures. Validating a Gaussian risk model for nine currencies, the test flags Brexit, COVID and other episodes; it extends to any null with computable, simulable conditionals.

Methodology.title: Scalable Estimation and Inference for Varying Coefficient Expectile Regression with Streaming Data
Methodology.summary: Nonparametric expectile regression methods face new challenges from streaming data, where retaining the full dataset for batch processing becomes increasingly impractical. In this paper, we develop a scalable nonparametric expectile regression framework for varying coefficient models. We estimate the coefficient functions online via functional stochastic gradient descent with Polyak--Ruppert averaging in a product reproducing kernel Hilbert space, requiring only gradient information and one pass over the data. For this online estimator, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds, prove its optimal nonparametric convergence rate under the proposed step-size schemes, and derive its Berry--Esseen bound for pointwise asymptotic normality. To perform online inference for the varying coefficient expectile regression models, we propose a multiplier bootstrap procedure that perturbs the stochastic gradients with independent random weights and recursively constructs bootstrap trajectories. We establish the bootstrap consistency of the online inference procedure, yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals. Simulation studies and a real data application confirm the performance of the proposed methods.

Methodology.title: FlexRL: an R package for Flexible Record Linkage and Linked Data Quality Assessment
Methodology.summary: FlexRL is an R package for probabilistic record linkage and inference on linked data. It provides a method to link observations from the same entities across two data sources that lack a unique identifier but share partially identifying variables. This method fits a hierarchical latent variable model of the data generation process, rather than classifying pairs of records from the comparison of their values, and accommodates registration errors and variables changing over time. Since linkage may affect subsequent analyses, the package also provides tools to assess the linked data quality as functions of the linkage decision rule. Two false discovery proportion estimators are implemented: a probabilistic approach contingent on the record linkage model and an augmented approach relying on an auxiliary estimation using synthetic data. Several measures of divergence of the linked sample from the source population are provided. These tools are agnostic to the underlying record linkage model and can be applied to any method. Together, they connect the output of the linkage to the validity of the subsequent analyses. The implementation combines standard R functions and S3 methods with Rcpp computations, resulting in fast execution times and a low memory footprint.
Methodology.comment: Published in the Journal of Reproducible Statistics

Methodology.title: A hybrid model for zero-inflated proportion data
Methodology.summary: This paper proposes a hybrid model for analyzing zero-inflated proportion data by distinguishing two types of zeros. The first type arises from sampling variability, whereas the second reflects intrinsically unsuitable covariates. Accordingly, the hybrid model combines a regression component for suitable observations with an estimator of the suitability region that identifies unsuitable covariates. Using a debiasing technique, we establish the consistency of both the regression and classification components, together with the asymptotic normality of the regression coefficient and a convergence rate for the support estimator. Comprehensive simulation studies verify our theoretical findings. We further apply the model to two real datasets, where it outperforms most competing methods.

Methodology.title: Debias Online Expectile Regression for High-Dimensional Stream Data and Statistic Inference
Methodology.summary: Expectile regression is a powerful tool for capturing heterogeneous structures in data and has attracted increasing attention in large-scale data analysis due to its computational efficiency. However, statistical inference for high-dimensional online expectile regression remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose a debiased online expectile regression method for high-dimensional streaming data. The proposed method incorporates Lasso regularization to perform variable selection and alleviate estimation instability caused by high dimensionality. It further adopts an online updating strategy in which recursively updated cumulative statistics are used to approximate the global gradient, and a proximal gradient descent algorithm is employed to update model parameters. To enable valid inference when only the current batch and historical summary statistics are available, we also develop an online precision matrix estimation procedure. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed debiased estimator. Extensive numerical studies and real-data applications show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to the oracle and offline estimators while maintaining low storage cost.

Methodology.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
Methodology.summary: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite this broad potential impact, selection bias is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct it, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle and assumptions, and we compare methods addressing the same form of selection by their assumptions, data requirements and limitations. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R, prepares input for the external SPREG software, and provides worked examples on simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection, one of which we present in full. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with recommendations for bias-aware study design, sensitivity analysis and reporting.

Methodology.title: Closed-form fractional radial links for elliptical Mahalanobis discriminant analysis
Methodology.summary: We study binary classification when the two classes are elliptical with a shared radial generator $g$. The log-likelihood ratio is then an additive function of the two squared Mahalanobis radii, with radial link $\varphi=\log g$. For Gaussian classes $\varphi$ is affine and the rule reduces to quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA); otherwise the Bayes link is not the identity. Instead of fitting this link with a spline smoother, we derive its family from the within-class law of the radius and estimate a finite fractional-power projection. We prove that the link is identifiable from the radius law, that the plug-in estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal under finite-moment conditions, and that the induced classifier is asymptotically Bayes-optimal in an iterated sieve limit. For $d\ge2$ and non-nested class parameters, the identity link suffices only for affine (Gaussian) generators. The bridge, GAM membership and the affine direction of this dichotomy are verified in Lean 4. We compare against the global Mahalanobis-GAM of Ghosh et al. (2025), re-implemented with mgcv REML splines at equal input budget. On two UCI benchmarks the derived link ties with the fitted GAM. On six financial series from three asset classes, with validation that respects temporal dependence, it is never significantly worse than the fitted GAM: better on CAD/USD and tied on the other five. It beats QDA on the three heaviest-tailed series (oil $[+0.023,+0.069]$, S&P 500 $[+0.039,+0.125]$, JPY/USD $[+0.009,+0.047]$) and ties elsewhere. A rate simulation with a closed-form ground truth reproduces the $\sqrt{n}$ rate and, under covariance heterogeneity, QDA's risk floor against the derived link's vanishing excess risk. The derived link thus matches a tuned GAM without smoothing-parameter selection and improves on QDA where the generator departs from the Gaussian.
Methodology.comment: 23 pages, 2 figures. v2: revised theory (CLT first-stage assumptions and two-step Jacobian, sieve theorem on class mixture, QDA risk-floor corollary, identity-link dichotomy proof for d>=2); abstract corrected to match tables; literature added; Lean list and reproducibility map in appendices. Code: https://github.com/SZabolotnii/DSGE-MV_Elliptical_LLR-code-supplement

Methodology.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model
Methodology.summary: This paper develops quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for genuinely unbalanced dynamic network panel data models. We first study a baseline one-way fixed effect specification and then extend the framework to two-way fixed effects. The model accommodates contemporaneous and lagged network spillovers, temporal dependence, and a listing effect that operates when a unit first appears in the panel. For the baseline specification, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the QMLE, characterize the incidental-parameter bias, and propose a bias-corrected estimator. We further provide a consistent estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix, to enable feasible inference. Under the two-way fixed effect extension, we derive the corresponding asymptotic distribution, bias correction, and covariance matrix estimator, accounting for the additional bias component induced by the time fixed effects. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators and inference procedure. An empirical application to Airbnb listings from New Zealand and New York City reveals region-specific patterns in spatial and temporal price transmission, highlighting the importance of modeling genuine unbalancedness in dynamic network settings.
Methodology.comment: Revised version. Adds a two-way fixed effects extension and feasible inference, updates the simulations and Airbnb application, and includes a supplementary appendix. Author order updated

Methodology.title: CausalCompass: Evaluating the Robustness of Time-Series Causal Discovery in Misspecified Scenarios
Methodology.summary: Causal discovery from time series is a fundamental task in machine learning. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by a reliance on untestable causal assumptions and by the lack of robustness-oriented evaluation in existing benchmarks. To address these challenges, we propose CausalCompass, a flexible and extensible benchmark framework designed to assess the robustness of time-series causal discovery (TSCD) methods under violations of modeling assumptions. To demonstrate the practical utility of CausalCompass, we conduct extensive benchmarking of representative TSCD algorithms across eight assumption-violation scenarios. Our experimental results indicate that no single method consistently attains optimal performance across all settings. Nevertheless, in most scenarios, the methods exhibiting superior overall performance are deep learning-based approaches. We further provide hyperparameter sensitivity analyses to deepen the understanding of these findings. We additionally conduct ablation experiments to explain the strong performance of deep learning-based methods under assumption violations. We also find that NTS-NOTEARS relies on standardized preprocessing in practice, performing poorly in the vanilla setting but exhibiting strong performance after standardization. Finally, our work aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of TSCD methods under assumption violations, thereby facilitating their broader adoption in real-world applications. The user-friendly implementation, documentation and datasets are available at https://github.com/huiyang-yi/CausalCompass.

Methodology.title: Optimal Forecast Reconciliation with Uncertainty Quantification
Methodology.summary: We propose to estimate the weight matrix used for forecast reconciliation as parameters in a general linear model in order to quantify its uncertainty. This implies that forecast reconciliation can be formulated as an orthogonal projection from the space of base-forecast errors into a coherent linear subspace. We use variance decomposition together with the Wishart distribution to derive the central estimator for the forecast-error covariance matrix. In addition, we prove that distance-reducing properties apply to the reconciled forecasts at all levels of the hierarchy as well as to the forecast-error covariance. A covariance matrix for the reconciliation weight matrix is derived, which leads to improved estimates of the forecast-error covariance matrix. We show how shrinkage can be introduced in the formulated model by imposing specific priors on the weight matrix and the forecast-error covariance matrix. The method is illustrated in a simulation study that shows consistent improvements in the log-score. Finally, standard errors for the weight matrix and the variance-separation formula are illustrated using a case study of forecasting electricity load in Sweden.

Methodology.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data
Methodology.summary: In permutation tests with discrete data, especially in small samples, different permutations often yield the same test statistic. The resulting ties can make the test conservative and reduce power. This conservatism can be particularly pronounced for maximum statistics: permutations may have the same maximum but differ at other endpoints, so the remaining endpoint statistics are discarded. We develop two power improvements for closed permutation maxT tests by refining the treatment of ties. The first method uses a single uniform random variable shared across all local tests in the closed testing procedure. This shared-uniform construction maximizes the rejection probability of every elementary hypothesis among all ways of coordinating the same randomized local tests. It also preserves an exact linear step-down shortcut. The second method is the deterministic two-endpoint augmentation (tea) test, which uses the second-largest endpoint statistic to resolve ties in the maximum. This additional information can favour rejection under alternatives while preserving null validity, without auxiliary randomization. Its full closure admits an exact quadratic shortcut. More generally, augmentation using any fixed number of endpoint statistics admits an exact polynomial shortcut. Both procedures retain every rejection made by classical closed maxT procedures and provide strong finite-sample control of the family-wise error rate under intersection-null permutation invariance. In simulations with sparse binary outcomes, both methods improve power over classical closed maxT testing. When many endpoints are tested, the tea test also often outperforms shared-uniform randomization.

Methodology.title: Coherent forecast combination for linearly constrained multiple time series
Methodology.summary: Forecasting linearly constrained multiple time series, as those arising in National Accounts, energy systems and supply chain planning, requires that the forecasts of all variables jointly satisfy the underlying accounting or resource-balance identities. When several experts provide forecasts for some or all of the variables, classical forecast combination operates on each variable and ignores the linear constraints, while forecast reconciliation enforces such constraints by using a single forecast per variable. To bridge this gap, we develop an original coherent forecast combination framework, in which the joint problem of combination across experts and coherence across variables is formulated as a linearly constrained optimization problem. Closed-form expressions are derived for the coherent combined forecast and its error covariance matrix, and the statistical properties of the resulting estimators are discussed. A Monte Carlo experiment and a forecasting application to an Australian daily electricity generation dataset confirm that the proposed approach significantly improves forecast accuracy with respect to standard forecast combination and reconciliation alternatives.

Methodology.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever
Methodology.summary: Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets---the data and code behind publications---in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal's reanalyses, years answering readers' questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal's reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit's hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record---confidential data included---without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.

Methodology.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors
Methodology.summary: Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) estimates directed effective connectivity, while parametric empirical Bayes (PEB) supports group inference using subject-specific posterior summaries. Standard PEB relies on Gaussian models and continuous shrinkage, making it sensitive to atypical estimates and unable to distinguish negligible from nonzero effects. We develop a robust and sparse group-DCM extension combining a Student-$t$ likelihood with a spike-and-slab prior using a nonlocal product-moment (pMOM) slab. A normal--gamma representation of the Student-$t$ distribution yields weights that downweight atypical {whitened residual coordinates}. The pMOM slab vanishes at zero, sharpening coefficient selection and yielding inclusion probabilities. {We propagate first-level posterior uncertainty through block-covariance pre-whitening and use a multistart generalized expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm with conditional maximization for mode fitting, followed by parallel-tempering posterior integration for inclusion probabilities. A simulation study showed that Student-$t$ weighting supplied the main protection against contamination, while spike-and-slab regularization reduced fixed-threshold false selections. In an openly shared mixed-gambles fMRI application, we found mild heterogeneity, concentrated inclusion support on departures of all four diagonal self-inhibition scaling parameters from the SPM default, and close directional agreement with standard PEB implemented in Statistical Parametric Mapping.} Our framework therefore adds interpretable {whitened-coordinate} robustness diagnostics and sparse coefficient selection to hierarchical DCM while retaining first-level uncertainty.

Methodology.title: postcard: An R Package for Marginal Effect Estimation with or without Prognostic Score Adjustment
Methodology.summary: Covariate adjustment is a widely used technique in randomized clinical trials (RCTs) for improving the efficiency of treatment effect estimators. By adjusting for predictive baseline covariates, variance can be reduced, enhancing statistical precision and study power. Rosenblum and van der Laan [2010] use the framework of generalized linear models (GLMs) in a plug-in analysis to show efficiency gains using covariate adjustment for marginal effect estimation. Recently the use of prognostic scores as adjustment covariates has gained popularity. Schuler et al. [2022] introduce and validate the method for continuous endpoints using linear models. Building on this work Højbjerre-Frandsen et al. [2025] extends the method proposed by Schuler et al. [2022] to be used in combination with the GLM plug-in procedure [Rosenblum and van der Laan, 2010]. This method achieves semi-parametric efficiency under assumptions of additive treatment effects on the link scale. Additionally, Højbjerre-Frandsen et al. [2025] provide a formula for power approximation which is valid even under model misspecification, enabling realistic sample size estimation. This article introduces an R package, which implements the GLM plug-in method with or without PrOgnoSTic CovARiate aDjustment, postcard. The package has two core features: (1) estimating marginal effects and the variance hereof (with or without prognostic adjustment) and (2) approximating statistical power. Functionalities also include integration of the Discrete Super Learner for constructing prognostic scores and simulation capabilities for exploring the methods in practice. Through examples and simulations, we demonstrate postcard as a practical toolkit for statisticians.

Methodology.title: Hypergraph Generation via Structured Stochastic Diffusion
Methodology.summary: Hypergraphs model higher-order interactions, but realistic hypergraph generation remains difficult because incidence, hyperedge-size heterogeneity, and overlap structure are not faithfully captured by pairwise reductions. We propose \HEDGE, a generative model defined directly on relaxed incidence matrices via a structured stochastic diffusion. The forward process combines a hypergraph-specific two-sided heat operator with an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck component, preserving structure-aware noising near the data while yielding an explicit Gaussian terminal law. Conditional on an observed hypergraph, this forward process is linear-Gaussian, so conditional means, covariances, scores, and reverse-drift targets are available in closed form. We therefore learn a permutation-equivariant state-only reverse-drift field in incidence space by regressing onto exact conditional targets, and generate samples by simulating a learned reverse-time SDE from the Gaussian base law. We establish exactness in the ideal state-only setting together with finite-horizon stability guarantees, and empirically show improved hypergraph generation quality relative to strong baselines.

Methodology.title: What is the Long-Term Value of Reliability?
Methodology.summary: We describe Chronos LTV, a system to measure the long-term impact of delays and other service defects on key business metrics. We use Markov decision processes to model customer interactions over time, and formalize our target estimand as the marginal policy effect with respect to moving the average delay rate. Given this setup, we show that we can identify long-term effects under a sequential unconfoundedness assumption where delays are as good as random given observed order characteristics; and can estimate these effects using a simple covariate-balancing algorithm.
Methodology.comment: Forthcoming in the Harvard Data Science Review

Methodology.title: Response-guided knockoffs for prespecified directional FDR control in linear models
Methodology.summary: Conventional false discovery rate (FDR) control limits the expected proportion of selected features that are unrelated to the response. Directional FDR extends this criterion to also account for incorrect sign estimates. In some applications, however, discoveries are sought only in a direction specified in advance. We therefore introduce the prespecified directional FDR, which counts as errors both null effects and effects opposite to the target direction in context of the fixed-design Gaussian linear model with unknown noise variance. A straightforward adaptation of the knockoff filter provides prespecified directional FDR control. To improve power, we develop the response-guided knockoff filter, which uses a noise-perturbed response to guide knockoff construction in favour of features likely to have the target sign, while retaining finite-sample prespecified directional FDR control. Notably, our improved filter maintains this guarantee with a sample size $n>p+2$ in contrast to standard constructions that require $n\geq2p$. Simulations across a range of settings demonstrate power gains of the response-guided knockoff filter. An application to HIV drug-resistance data illustrates improved recovery of externally annotated resistance-associated mutations.

Methodology.title: Supervised Factor-Augmented Matrix Regression with Weak Factors
Methodology.summary: We develop a supervised factor-augmented matrix regression framework for high-dimensional analysis with weak factors. When factor loadings are concentrated on unknown subsets of rows and columns, conventional full-matrix factor extraction may suffer substantial signal dilution, with weakness in one matrix dimension propagating to estimation in the other. We characterize this two-way weak-loading phenomenon for both \(α\)-PCA and projected estimators and show that their loading and factor estimates may deteriorate under weak signals. To address this problem, we propose a sequential response-guided screening procedure that identifies informative rows and columns prior to factor extraction. We establish exact support recovery and show that post-screening factor re-estimation converts the weak-loading problem into a pervasive one relative to the retained dimensions, yielding sharper convergence rates under substantially weaker dimensional growth conditions and consistent factor-number determination. We further establish asymptotic distributions for both unrestricted and bilinear regression estimators based on the estimated matrix factors. Simulations demonstrate substantial improvements in support recovery and factor estimation under weak signals. We illustrate the gains obtained by the response-guided factor construction with two empirical applications.

Methodology.title: Advection-aligned block Vecchia inference for spatio-temporal Gaussian processes
Methodology.summary: Vecchia approximations enable scalable likelihood-based inference for large Gaussian process models, but their accuracy depends on the choice of conditioning sets. For spatio-temporal processes with advection, target-centered conditioning can omit informative past observations. Motivated by total column ozone observations from the Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS), we propose a data-driven, advection-aligned block Vecchia approximation that incorporates estimated transport direction into temporal conditioning geometry. Observation locations need not lie on a regular grid. An initial advection vector is estimated from the data and used once to select transport-aligned past-time conditioning blocks. The resulting graph is held fixed during optimization, while covariance and advection parameters remain free to vary. This separates neighbor selection from covariance estimation, avoids repeated parameter-dependent neighbor searches, and provides an interpretable connection between conditioning geometry and estimated transport. Batched graphics processing unit (GPU) operations evaluate the likelihood and its gradients. In a matched comparison of daily GEMS datasets from July 2024 and July 2025, advection-aligned conditioning attained a lower fitted Vecchia negative log-likelihood than target-centered conditioning on 53 of 61 days. In six Matérn simulation scenarios with 120 matched eight-hour fields each, advection-aligned conditioning reduced advection-vector root mean squared error relative to target-centered conditioning at the same conditioning-block budget, with the largest reduction under strong transport.

Methodology.title: Guidance for Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation
Methodology.summary: Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) serves as a vital framework for parameter inference in scientific fields where simulators involve intractable likelihoods, yet while amortized generative models offer rapid posterior estimation, they are often restricted by the specific priors used during training, thereby limiting their flexibility as prior knowledge evolves. To address this prior dependency, PriorGuide was introduced as an inference-time guidance method, but due to its intractable formulation, it relies on Gaussian approximations of the reverse transition kernel and Gaussian mixture model fitting for the prior ratio, both of which introduce systematic bias. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an unbiased test-time guidance framework that leverages Density Ratio Estimation (DRE) to learn a score guidance term, effectively decoupling the inference process from the prior training. Moreover, our framework remains agnostic to the specific density ratio estimators, making it a general and flexible framework for handling prior changes. Experimental results across multiple tasks demonstrate that our method matches or outperforms PriorGuide on C2ST and MMD in most tasks while maintaining robustness even under limited overlap between the training and target priors. Furthermore, we apply our method to Bayesian updating for parameter inference from planetary light-curve data, where it also demonstrates strong effectiveness and robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/a-chenchen/dre-based-prior-guidance .

Methodology.title: Competitive Balance Beyond Standings: Bayesian Inference for Latent Tiers and Structural Heterogeneity
Methodology.summary: Competitive balance has long been a central concern in sports economics, tied to outcome uncertainty, fan engagement, and the way leagues design their policies. Most existing measures of competitive balance are built from standings or winning percentages, which say little about how overall parity relates to the way teams sort into latent competitive tiers. We propose a Bayesian framework based on the Bradley-Terry model that jointly estimates the number of competitive tiers and team memberships. To capture the overall degree of competitive heterogeneity, we introduce a structural balance parameter defined on the unit interval within a hierarchical model, and we establish theoretical results giving this parameter a clear interpretation:it is directly tied to the separation between tiers, and overall heterogeneity depends on both the size and frequency of cross-tier differences. Importantly, structural balance is distinct from the information content of the schedule itself, so leagues with different numbers of teams and games can be compared on equal footing. Inference is carried out with an efficient posterior sampling algorithm that jointly handles team abilities, tier structure, home advantage, and structural balance. Simulation studies validate the proposed method, showing accurate recovery of the latent competitive structure and correct performance of the structural-balance testing procedure. Applied to the NBA and NFL, it reveals that the two leagues exhibit similar global structural balance despite very different competitive organizations: the NBA has three latent tiers, while the NFL has two broader ones, and the NFL's sparser schedule produces considerably more posterior uncertainty. Overall parity, it turns out, can mask quite different forms of competitive stratification-something standings-based measures alone cannot detect.

Methodology.title: Bayesian Unit-level Quantile Modeling with Application to Wealth Data
Methodology.summary: Modeling wealth quantiles over time and space and across fine-grained demographic classifications is of vital importance to policy makers. However, such data present unique challenges for standard small area estimation methodologies because they are highly skewed and heavy-tailed with both positive and negative values. Traditional area-level modeling and design-based approaches struggle to capture these features. Meanwhile, existing unit-level methodology frequently treats the survey design as ignorable and does not apply to surveys that are repeated over time. Often the analysis is restricted to alternative response variables that are non-negative, such as poverty indicators or income. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Bayesian, asymmetric Laplace pseudolikelihood model that is able to capture the major features of wealth while adjusting for survey weights and accounting for both spatial and temporal dependence. We present a Gibbs sampling algorithm for our model, as well as a variational Bayes algorithm for fast computation. We apply the method to the Survey of Income and Program Participation to characterize geographic, temporal, and demographic variation in the distribution of U.S. household wealth, including for sparsely sampled domains where direct estimates are unavailable or unstable.

Methodology.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness
Methodology.summary: Clinical notes contain rich patient information, such as diagnoses or medications, making them valuable for patient representation learning. Recent advances in large language models have further improved the ability to extract meaningful representations from clinical texts. However, clinical notes are often missing. For example, in our MIMIC-IV cohort, 35.15% of patients have no eligible discharge summaries. In such cases, representations can be learned from other modalities such as structured data, chest X-rays, or radiology reports. Yet the availability of these modalities is influenced by clinical decision-making and varies across patients, potentially producing modality missing-not-at-random (MMNAR) patterns. We propose a causal representation learning framework that leverages observed data and informative missingness in multimodal clinical records. It consists of: (1) an MMNAR-aware modality fusion component that integrates structured data, imaging, and text while conditioning on missingness patterns to capture patient health and clinician-driven assignment; (2) a modality reconstruction component with latent alignment to preserve modality information in the learned representation; and (3) a multitask outcome prediction model with a rectifier that corrects for residual bias from specific modality observation patterns. Comprehensive evaluations across MIMIC-IV and eICU show consistent gains over the strongest baselines, achieving relative AUC improvements of up to 4.3% for hospital readmission and 2.7% for ICU admission.
Methodology.comment: To appear in Proc. of EMNLP 2025 (21 pages)

Graphics.title: Real-Time Self-Penetration Repair for Skinned Characters with Soft Contact Budgets
Graphics.summary: Motion that is plausible on one body can penetrate another after a change in shape, and motion models can produce self-penetration on their native characters. We present a training-free post-process that reduces these artifacts through pose correction followed by bounded skin compression. The module attaches to any motion model whose native character and output character have compatible character packs, without access to model internals. Each pack is built offline from the rig and skin without training. A vertex-level pose layer solves a local quadratic program in plain C on one CPU core, and a stateless contact deformer acts on the host's final skinned mesh. A part-dependent soft-tissue budget allocates correction between pose and skin through a static convention. Source penetration contributes no extra allowance; optional cloth thickness and compliance modify the pose layer's collision surface. Operation is causal or uses a short buffered lookahead, with frame-exact pass-through at the native interface for clean, inactive frames in the zero state. Across 320 unseen clips and 3 body shapes, the fraction of frames with hand-torso depth above 20 mm falls from 15.53% for copied motion to 0.00%, with final maximum depth 9.3 mm over every frame. Mean pose and skin costs are 1.11 and 1.18 ms, respectively, and their sum of 2.29 ms is a sub-frame processing cost. The median joint-velocity high-frequency ratio relative to copied target motion is 1.008.

Graphics.title: Audiovisual Disparities in VR: Impact on Spatial Perception
Graphics.summary: Virtual reality (VR) experiences often leverage rich and spatialized multimodal environments to increase immersion and engagement. This demands a consistent spatial perception of audiovisual stimuli, since perceived discrepancies can disrupt the sense of presence. In this work, we investigate the consequences of two types of spatial audiovisual disparities: true disparity, where there is a measurable spatial offset between auditory and visual cues, and perceptual disparity, where users report misalignment despite cues being colocated. Unlike most previous studies that employed controlled but simplified experimental setups, our research focuses on complex, realistic VR environments, allowing us to assess the actual implications for VR content design. Our experiments indicate that users are highly sensitive to true audiovisual disparities in controlled environments, detecting even minor misalignments. However, when engaged in additional tasks within realistic settings, their ability to notice such discrepancies diminishes significantly. We also observed that previously found perceptual disparities persist in complex audiovisual environments. However, we identify self-initiated head rotations as a key factor; its absence prevents the effect entirely. We hope our findings offer practical insights for designing more immersive and perceptually coherent VR experiences.
Graphics.comment: 2025 IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR)

Graphics.title: The Drawing You Watch Is the Portrait You Keep: A Replayable Machine Portrait Studio
Graphics.summary: Ask an image model for your portrait and a finished picture arrives: no first line, no second thoughts, no record of how it got there, and a different picture if you ask again. I built a portrait studio that works the other way. A sitter chooses one of eight fictional artists, each written with a city, a medium and a tempo of its own, holds still for 8 to 12 seconds, and watches a drawing of themselves appear over 44 seconds. One still is sent after consent, a hosted image model returns a private study the sitter never sees, and a compiler turns that study into one drawing document. The live drawing, the saved sheet, the vector export and the film all read that document, and a replay makes no model call, so the drawing you watch is the portrait you keep. I describe the compiler in enough detail to rebuild it and say plainly what it is: an authored reconstruction at a compressed speed, not a recorded hand. On 16 generated test studies a sheet holds 8,784 to 16,378 timed contacts, about three quarters of them fixed-grid fills and nearly all shorter than one video frame, and recompiling one study gave byte-identical output four times on one machine. The paper also traces a bug that matters more than any of that. The earlier compiler estimated the paper colour tile by tile, read dark skin as paper, and in all eight hands kept less of a deep-complexioned face than a fair one (13 to 48 percent against 41 to 56). On 80 generated studies the rebuilt engine keeps the complexion difference the study already has (raw retention 89 to 120 percent), so the fairness question has moved upstream, to the study and the hosted model. The two test sitters are generated and differ in more than complexion, and no real-face or perceptual study exists yet. The studio is live at https://everyfaceproject.com.
Graphics.comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 9 tables. Live system: https://everyfaceproject.com

Graphics.title: RigidFormer: Learning Rigid Dynamics using Transformers
Graphics.summary: Learning-based simulation of multi-object rigid-body dynamics remains difficult because contact is discontinuous and errors compound over long horizons. Most existing methods remain tied to mesh connectivity and vertex-level message passing, which limits their applicability to mesh-free inputs such as point clouds and leads to high computational cost. Efficiently modeling high-fidelity rigid-body dynamics from mesh-free representations therefore remains challenging. We introduce RigidFormer, an object-centric Transformer-based model that learns mesh-free rigid-body dynamics with controllable integration step sizes. RigidFormer reasons at the object level and advances each object through compact anchors; Anchor-Vertex Pooling enriches these anchors with local vertex features, retaining contact-relevant geometry without dense vertex-level interaction. We propose Anchor-based RoPE to make attention aware of the objects' spatial layout while respecting the unordered nature of objects and anchors: object-token processing is permutation-equivariant, and the mean-pooled anchor descriptor is invariant to anchor reindexing. RigidFormer further enforces rigidity by projecting updates onto the rigid-body manifold using differentiable Kabsch alignment. On standard benchmarks, RigidFormer outperforms or matches mesh-based baselines using point inputs, runs faster, generalizes to unseen point resolutions and across datasets, and scales to 200+ objects; we also show a preliminary extension to command-conditioned articulated bodies by treating body parts as interacting object-level components. Project page: https://frank-zy-dou.github.io/projects/RigidFormer/

Graphics.title: Segmenting Geometric Textures of 3D Meshes
Graphics.summary: Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.

Graphics.title: Refining and Repairing Signed Distance Data With Global Consistency
Graphics.summary: We propose a method to interpolate exact Signed Distance Function (SDF) data from a discrete set of samples. Unlike prior work, our approach ensures that the new SDF data values are fully consistent with the input and each other, such that the augmented data still corresponds to a geometrically realizable surface. We express the theoretical properties of exact SDFs as hard geometric constraints, and construct an efficient greedy algorithm for consistent SDF interpolation that is made even faster with powerful parallelized GPU preprocessing. We exemplify the usefulness of our method by evaluating it on three practical applications: global SDF refinement, in which the SDF data is upsampled without knowledge of the ground truth; mesh reconstruction, where our method can reconstruct highly detailed surfaces using global information from coarse input SDFs; and repair of pseudo-SDFs, which result from many pipelines such as CSG Boolean operations and must be turned into valid SDFs for downstream processing tasks. Our refined SDFs are guaranteed to be consistent with the input, where previous methods have no such guarantee.

Graphics.title: DC-SQEM: Medial Mesh Extraction by Dual Contouring with Spherical Quadric Error Metric
Graphics.summary: The medial axis, as a compact representation, describes not only the boundary but also the interior of the shape, and has been widely used in analyzing and simplifying shapes. However, approximating feature-preserving medial axis from unstructured data, such as oriented point clouds, remains challenging due to the lack of explicit connectivity and the presence of noise in the source. We propose DC-SQEM, a dual-contouring-based framework that computes medial meshes (an explicit representation of the medial axis) directly from oriented point clouds without relying on watertight manifold surfaces or volumetric structures. With the help of an adaptive octree, our method fits local medial spheres for each cell based on the Spherical Quadric Error Metric (SQEM). We address several long-standing robustness issues in dual-contouring and mesh extraction, including out-of-cell solutions, unstable feature classification, and redundant topological connections. To this end, we introduce virtual nodes, a feature-downgrading strategy, and a geometry-driven topology-aware cleanup procedure, enabling robust SQEM-based medial dual contouring with clean mesh outputs. Unlike prior point-cloud-based methods that produce either only 1D skeletal structures or incomplete medial features, our method preserves sharp geometric features from the input and reconstructs a complete medial structure, including sheets, curves, seams, and junctions. Compared to restricted-power-diagram-based approaches, our algorithm can handle point clouds as input, without having a strong requirement on water-tightness or manifoldness.

Graphics.title: Incremental Matrix Assembly for Preplanned Dynamic Tetrahedral Meshes
Graphics.summary: Local topology edits require updating assembled operators even when most of a tetrahedral mesh remains unchanged. We implement and evaluate incremental matrix assembly for preplanned edits, assuming a fixed pool of candidate elements with precomputable contributions. A preallocated sparse layout allows operator values to be updated from edited elements without rebuilding the sparsity structure. We compare full reassembly, local recomputation, and persistent incremental updates using a shared layout. Across tested meshes with up to 460k tetrahedra, incremental assembly achieves 6-27 times assembly speedups over a vectorized full-reassembly baseline for a proxy graph Laplacian and 2-17 times for linear elasticity. Frame times decrease by 1-3% when the linear solve dominates and by 18-20% in the tested synthetic dynamic elasticity loop with shorter solves. Local Recompute often achieves comparable frame times. For fixed time-step coefficients, directly maintaining the combined elasticity system also avoids a global matrix-combination pass. The Laplacian matches full reconstruction exactly in every tested frame; elasticity differences remain at rounding scale, reaching a maximum entry difference of 4.2 times 10^(-16) over 5,000 frames.
Graphics.comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Revision: updated title and framing, corrected performance claims and added baseline comparisons, numerical validation, and additional experiments

Graphics.title: Same Pixels, Different Documents: Measuring Part-Level Editability in Image Vectorization
Graphics.summary: Image vectorization is often evaluated by rendering fidelity, which cannot distinguish documents that render identically but support different edits. Edit-based evaluation tests outcomes, but an oracle that gathers a part's fragments can conceal the cost of selecting them. We introduce Pass@k, which tests whether a prescribed edit can succeed using objects selectable within k clicks under a specified interaction model. Eight document diagnostics characterize properties relevant to editing beyond these tasks. We assess structural sensitivity through controlled perturbations, practical relevance through designer operations, and reference dependence through alternative drawings. We evaluate twelve open and commercial methods on 211 references, with 635 edit tasks on 93 of them. In each of four reference sets, including two drawn by designers, 64-88% of oracle-passed tasks on parts composed of multiple shapes fail at Pass@1, against 6-40% for single shapes, pooling counts over configurations. Higher fidelity does not guarantee higher Pass@1, while selected diagnostics are associated with designers' effort in our study.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual understanding, yet the internal features that cause these behaviors remain difficult to identify, audit, or control. While applicable to post-hoc inspection, hidden states that are decomposed into interpretable feature directions using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) neither readily isolate which features are changed by multimodal training, nor are they directly useful for targeted control. We introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework that trains multimodal SAEs and turns them into feature-level interfaces for discovering and controlling multimodal behavior. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. We train multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families, LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5, and evaluate on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and OCR. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. These results show that multimodal SAEs can serve not only as interpretability tools, but as mechanisms for auditing, steering, and controlling MLLMs behavior toward safer and more capable generations.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Artificial Intelligence.title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
Artificial Intelligence.summary: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
Artificial Intelligence.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 55 pages. Project page: https://codiscovery.ai/contrastive-discovery/

Artificial Intelligence.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to KDD 2026, Jeju, Korea. 9 pages, 3 figures

Artificial Intelligence.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many. These findings point to concrete design principles for autoresearch systems: since models can judge candidates they cannot produce, enriching the search with externally sourced ideas and questions may be more effective than improving any single model's generation ability.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
Artificial Intelligence.summary: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 31 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables, including references and appendices

Artificial Intelligence.title: Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward: Towards Principled One-step Generator RL
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Recent advances in one-step text-to-image generation have enabled real-time synthesis with remarkable efficiency and quality. Previous reinforcement learning methods for one-step generators combine image-space reward optimization with diffusion noisy-space distribution matching. This paradigm brings challenges due to a mismatch between terminal reward optimization and the underlying generative dynamics. As a result, optimization tends to exploit stochastic degrees of freedom, often improving reward at the expense of image fidelity. To address this issue, we propose Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward (DIDR), a data-free trajectory-level alignment framework derived from Integral KL minimization. DIDR propagates the RLHF-optimal reward-tilted clean-image distribution across all noise levels along the diffusion trajectory. We show that this objective admits the same minimizer as clean-image RLHF, while naturally inducing the Diffused Reward Score (DRS), which acts as a reward-driven correction to the reference score function. To make this practical, we further introduce the Diffused Reward Proxy (DRP), an efficient estimator of DRS based on differentiable short-step denoising. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DIDR consistently Pareto-dominates existing one-step SDXL baselines. Moreover, when transferred to a 6B DiT backbone (Z-Image), DIDR surpasses its 50-step teacher in preference alignment while requiring only a single generation step. Code: https://github.com/Junyi-W/DIDR
Artificial Intelligence.comment: 33 pages. Updated manuscript and author information

Artificial Intelligence.title: SupplyNetPy: An Open-Source Python Library for High-Fidelity Modeling and Simulation of Arbitrary Supply Chain and Inventory Networks
Artificial Intelligence.summary: This paper introduces SupplyNetPy, an open-source, well-documented Python library for modeling and discrete-event simulation of supply chain networks with arbitrary multi-echelon structures. It supports multiple replenishment policies, perishable inventory, node disruptions, and stochastic demand and lead times. All components are extensible via inheritance. Users describe a supply chain as a graph with node and link attributes, while the library handles simulation, providing logs and extensive node and network level performance reports. This paper presents the motivation, design, key features, and architecture of SupplyNetPy, along with detailed validation results (against analytical benchmarks, a commercial tool, and a published case study). A key motivation behind SupplyNetPy's development is programmatic generation and simulation of complex models, enabling design-space exploration, what-if analysis, training data generation, and supply chain digital twins.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: Accepted to the Winter Simulation Conference 2026

Artificial Intelligence.title: From AGI to ASI
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Over the last decade, building human-level artificial general intelligence has moved from far-fetched speculation to being a concrete next-decade target for many of the largest AI organizations. Achieving this goal would have profound and far-reaching impacts on human society, which raises many complex questions for the decade ahead. This report investigates how AI itself might continue to develop in a post-AGI world along the continuum of machine intelligence. The endpoint of this continuum, Universal AI, is theoretically well understood, which provides some formal grounding for the main focus of this report: the transition from human-level AGI to artificial general superintelligence, which can intuitively be understood as a system that is more intelligent and cognitively capable than large organizations of humans. After characterizing ASI, the report discusses four potential pathways from AGI to ASI: scaling AGI, AI paradigm shifts, ASI emerging from large-scale multi-agent collectives, and recursive improvement. The report then discusses possible frictions and bottlenecks along these pathways. Determining whether the impact of these frictions will be negligible or substantial raises a number of concrete open research questions. While large uncertainties for predicting ASI progress remain, it cannot be ruled out that AI progress might continue to accelerate over the next years. This would imply that the image of a single transformative step change, caused by the introduction of human-level AGI into our society, could be inaccurate. More apt might be the prospect of a series of transformative societal changes caused by AI-enabled progress and breakthroughs across many areas of science and technology. Preparing for this prospect requires a massively interdisciplinary endeavor of global scope and interest.
Artificial Intelligence.comment: v3: minor fixes, overhaul of RSI mechanisms, and addition cognitive industrialization

Artificial Intelligence.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
Artificial Intelligence.summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Two Communities, One Problem: Branch-and-Bound vs. A* for Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling
Artificial Intelligence.summary: Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and $A^*$ are popular exact search methods originating from Operations Research and Artificial Intelligence, respectively. Although the two methods share fundamental search principles, their different ways of exploring the search space can lead to substantially different computational performance. We investigate these differences using the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP) as an exemplary problem setting. We first establish the relationships between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations.
