Finally, rotating Nariai data admit the required spacelike graph throughout the regular branch; an all-order tensor estimate yields smooth Kerr--de Sitter or rotating-Nariai rigidity for $a^2/r_0^2\leq1/8$, without assuming ambient axial symmetry.

Differential Geometry.title: Bounded Harmonic Functions on Products with a Parabolic Factor
Differential Geometry.summary: We prove that if $M$ is a connected complete parabolic Riemannian manifold and $N$ is a connected complete stochastically complete Riemannian manifold, then every bounded harmonic function on $M\times N$ is independent of the $M$-variable. Equivalently, pullback by the second projection induces an isometric isomorphism from the space of bounded harmonic functions on $N$ onto that on $M\times N$. In particular, the product of two parabolic manifolds has the bounded Liouville property, thereby answering Problem~16 of Grigor'yan's survey in the affirmative. The key analytic input is a total-variation memory-loss property of the heat kernel on a parabolic manifold. We establish this property by showing that the time-one heat kernel defines an aperiodic Harris recurrent transition kernel and then applying the row-merging theorem of Jamison and Orey.
Differential Geometry.comment: 13 pages. v2: acknowledgments added. v3: author affiliation and contact information added; minor corrections and clarifications. Comments are welcome!

Differential Geometry.title: Classification of 3-dimensional complex nilmanifolds - Teichmüller and moduli spaces
Differential Geometry.summary: We classify complex nilmanifolds of dimension three by describing the Teichmüller and moduli spaces of left-invariant complex structures for every real six-dimensional nilmanifold.

Differential Geometry.title: Global Classification of the Flat Singular Escobar-Yamabe Equation
Differential Geometry.summary: In every dimension $n\geq3$, we classify positive solutions of the flat Escobar--Yamabe equation on the Euclidean half-space with a possible isolated boundary singularity at the origin. Solutions with a removable singularity are boundary bubbles. Up to dilation, the nonremovable solutions are the cylindrical solution and a family of periodic Delaunay solutions uniquely parametrized by the necksize $ε\in (0,1)$, the minimum of the normalized boundary trace. In each fundamental period $T_ε$, the trace has exactly two critical points, a nondegenerate minimum and a nondegenerate maximum. The period and the solution centered at the trace minimum and rescaled to period one depend smoothly on $ε$. As $ε\to 0$, $T_ε= \frac{4}{n-2}\log(1/ε)+O(1)$. As $ε\to 1$, the solutions converge to the cylindrical solution and their periods tend to that of its linearized oscillation. We use uniqueness in the odd and even classes for linear Robin equations to obtain reflection symmetry and continuation in the necksize.

Differential Geometry.title: Gamma classes, central connection matrices, and tt* geometry
Differential Geometry.summary: We review the gamma class of complex projective space, but from the point of view of topological-antitopological fusion. We deconstruct the central connection matrix which appears in the work of Dubrovin, Galkin-Golyshev-Iritani, and Cotti-Dubrovin-Guzzetti.

Differential Geometry.title: Harmonic functions and comparsion geometry for noncompact 3-manifolds with nonnegative scalar curvature
Differential Geometry.summary: In this paper, we establish several sharp comparsion results for noncompact 3-manifolds with nonnegative scalar curvature and with a compact, connected boundary under a boundary mean curvature condition. Then we apply these gradient estimates to establish a Cohn-Vossen type bound for the average of the scalar curvature. This generalizes the work of Colding-Minicozzi \cite{Cold4} and Oronzio \cite{Oro2}.

Differential Geometry.title: Ricci pseudo symmetric Anisotropic Fluid Spacetime admitting Hyperbolic solitons with Ricci vector field
Differential Geometry.summary: This work focuses on an anisotropic fluid spacetime with these unique forms of the stress-energy tensor associated with radial pressure and a transverse pressure p. In an anisotropic fluid spacetime , we mani- fest curvatures symmetry such as Ricci pseudo-symmetric and prove that Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime is generalized quasi- Einstein spacetime. We deduce the Einstein gravitational field equation of Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime. In the framework of pseudo-Riemannian geometry, specifically, we study the quasi-conformal Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime, which exhibit the dark matter era. Moreover, we discuss the hyperbolic Ricci soliton and Hyperbolic Yamabe soliton on Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime with a time-like Ricci vector field. Finally, we turn up the char- acteristics of hyperbolic Ricci soliton and hyperbolic Yamabe soliton on Ricci pseudo-symmetric anisotropic fluid spacetime with a time-like Ricci vector field.

Differential Geometry.title: $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$- and $\mathfrak{osp}(1|2)$-invariant multidifferential operators
Differential Geometry.summary: We determine the dimension of the space of $\mathfrak{sl}(2)$-invariant (n)-ary differential operators on weighted densities for arbitrary weights, including the singular cases in which the usual elimination procedure breaks down. The proof relies on the strong Lefschetz property established by Stanley \cite{s} and Watanabe \cite{w}. We also investigate the corresponding problem in the super case.

Differential Geometry.title: Fractal solutions to the two-dimensional floating body problem
Differential Geometry.summary: In this paper, the first construction of an entire class of two-dimensional fractal bodies that float in water in equilibrium is explicitly given. Their boundaries are described by planar fractal Zindler curves which are constructed using fractal projective hedgehogs. The areas of these bodies are seen to be well-defined and their expression is explicitly computed. To this end, a result concerning the continuity of the Lebesgue measure with respect to the Hausdorff metric for compact sets is given. Furthermore, the Hausdorff dimension $w$ of these fractal curves is shown to coincide with the Hausdorff dimension of the graph of a Weierstrass function associated to the corresponding fractal projective hedgehog. The fractal Zindler curves are proved to have halving chords of constant length that split both the area and the $w$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of the curve into exact halves.

Differential Geometry.title: A Complex Structure on A Rational Homology Six-Sphere with Two-Torsion
Differential Geometry.summary: We construct a compact, smooth, simply connected complex threefold. Its second and third integral homology groups are cyclic of order two, and its remaining homology groups agree with those of the six-sphere.

Differential Geometry.title: Conserved quantities of distinguished curves on conformal sphere
Differential Geometry.summary: We give conserved quantities of two generalizations of conformal circles on the conformal sphere. One generalization concerns curves carrying a distinguished parallel tractor along them, which can be used to construct the conserved quantities. The other is the class of curves satisfying the conformal Mercator equation, the conserved quantities of which are computed using Lagrangian formalism. The two generalizations are not disjoint, and our main result is the relation between their conserved quantities. Explicit examples are also presented.
Differential Geometry.comment: Accepted for publication in Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications (J. Math. Anal. Appl. 568 (2027) 131161)

Differential Geometry.title: On the limit of simply connected manifolds with discrete isometric cocompact group actions
Differential Geometry.summary:
We study the fundamental group of the equivariant Gromov--Hausdorff limit space \[ (M_i, p_i, G_i) \xrightarrow{eGH} (Y, p, G), \] where $\{(M_i,p_i)\}_{i\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence of complete, connected, and simply connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifolds with $\mathrm{Ric}\ge -(n-1)$. Here $G_i\subset \mathrm{Iso}(M_i)$ is a discrete subgroup satisfying $\mathrm{diam}(M_i/G_i)\le D$ for some fixed constant $D>0$.
  Let $G_0$ denote the identity component of $G$. Then $G_0$ is a nilpotent Lie group. Let $T^k \subseteq G_0$ be the maximal torus.
  Our main result asserts that the quotient space $Y/T^k$ is simply connected. Moreover, the fundamental group $π_1(Y,p)$ is generated, up to conjugation, by loops contained in $T^k$-orbits. More precisely, each generator can be represented by a loop of the form \begin{equation*} γ= α\cdot β\cdot α^{-1}, \end{equation*} where $α$ is a curve from $p$ to some point $y \in Y$, and $β$ is a loop based at $y$ that lies entirely in the $T^k$-orbit of $y$.

Differential Geometry.title: Non-collapsed RCD spaces with local bounded covering geometry
Differential Geometry.summary:
We study non-collapsed $\mathrm{RCD}(-(N-1),N)$ spaces with locally bounded covering geometry.
  Our first main result generalizes Gromov's almost flat manifold theorem: if the universal cover is non-collapsing and the diameter is sufficiently small, then the space is bi-Holder homeomorphic to an infranilmanifold. In the smooth setting with $\mathrm{Ric} \ge -(N-1)$, this homeomorphism is actually a diffeomorphism. As an application of our arguments, we show that Gromov's almost flat manifold theorem extends to the $\mathrm{RCD}+\mathrm{CBA}$ setting.
  Our second main result generalizes Fukaya's fibration theorem. Suppose a sequence of non-collapsed $\mathrm{RCD}(-(N-1),N)$ spaces with locally bounded covering geometry converges in the pointed measured Gromov--Hausdorff sense to a smooth manifold of dimension $k < N$. We then construct a topological fiber bundle map from the RCD spaces to the limit manifold. The fibers are infranilmanifolds, and the structure group is affine.
  Finally, although there exist collapsing Ricci limit spaces with no topological manifold points, we prove that if the sequence additionally satisfies locally bounded covering geometry and the limit space has dimension $k$, then every $k$-regular point is a topological manifold point.

Differential Geometry.title: Bott--Chern and Aeppli Cohomology of toroidal groups
Differential Geometry.summary: We compute the Bott--Chern and Aeppli cohomology groups of theta toroidal groups in arbitrary dimensions, obtaining explicit dimension formulas and bases in all bidegrees. For general toroidal groups, we determine the Hausdorff reductions of these cohomology groups and show that they coincide with those of theta toroidal groups. We also compute the Bott--Chern and Aeppli cohomology groups themselves in certain specific bidegrees, without passing to their Hausdorff reductions.

Differential Geometry.title: A second-order estimate linear in the gradient for complex Hessian equations
Differential Geometry.summary: We use the maximum principle to prove a second-order estimate with linear dependence on the gradient for the nondegenerate complex Hessian equation on a compact Kähler manifold. The proof combines $C^0$ compactness and a refined concavity inequality with the use of nearby smooth admissible functions. A standard interpolation argument then yields the known uniform gradient and complex Hessian bounds.

Differential Geometry.title: Local study of generic dynamical systems on the b-symplectic plane
Differential Geometry.summary: Let $\Gb$ be the group of germs of planar diffeomorphisms, fixing the origin, which preserve the standard b-symplectic form. The group acts on itself, under the usual left-right action and we identify, in the generic case, a simple representative of each orbit, depending on a non-vanishing, univariate, function. We then study the action of $\Gb$ on b-symplectic vector fields. For those fields that do not vanish at the origin, we establish a flow-box type theorem, while, for those that do vanish there, we show that the study of their conjugacy classes reduces to a classification of functions. We present this classification, when the origin is a regular point for these functions, while if it is a critical point, we present the orbits of their 2-jets. Finally, we address the problem of whether an element of $\Gb$ can be realised as the time-1 map of a b-symplectic vector field.
Differential Geometry.comment: 23 pages, keywords: b-symplectic plane, classification of dynamical systems

Differential Geometry.title: Stochastic Parallel Transport along Markov Processes: I. General Theory
Differential Geometry.summary: We give a framework for transporting vectors along Markov processes that may have jumps, without assuming a manifold or other specific geometric structure. We prove existence and uniqueness of the resulting transport. In doing so, we develop a theory of vector bundles defined quasi-everywhere, in which the vectors live, and an axiomatic framework for energy forms that determine the bundle and the transport.

Differential Geometry.title: The Escobar Constant for Two-dimensional Disks
Differential Geometry.summary: Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth compact Riemannian surface homeomorphic to a closed disk, with boundary length $L$. We establish sharp upper bounds for its Escobar constant under upper bounds on the Gaussian curvature. If $K_g\leq 0$, then $I(M,g)\leq 2/π$, with equality if and only if $(M,g)$ is isometric to a Euclidean disk. If $K_g\leqκ$ for some $κ>0$, $L<2π/\sqrtκ$, and $\operatorname{Area}_g(M)<2π/κ$, then $I(M,g)\leq\frac{4}{\sqrtκL}\arcsin(\frac{\sqrtκL}{2π})$, with equality if and only if $(M,g)$ is isometric to the geodesic disk of the same perimeter contained in an open hemisphere of the sphere of constant curvature $κ$. We also discuss the higher order Escobar constant for planar domains. In particular, we construct counterexamples to Hassannezhad and Siffert's conjecture.

Differential Geometry.title: Jacobi fields and Jacobi sections for semisprays on Lie algebroids: transverse variations and equivalences
Differential Geometry.summary: We study the relationship between Jacobi sections and Jacobi fields associated with semisprays on Lie algebroids. First, we characterize compatible transverse variations in terms of Lie algebroid morphisms. This characterization leads to a variational description of Jacobi sections: a section along an integral curve of a semispray is a Jacobi section if and only if it arises as the infinitesimal variation of a compatible transverse variation of a dynamical variation satisfying a suitable condition on its image in the base. We also investigate the relationship between Jacobi sections and Jacobi fields through the anchor map. We prove that every Jacobi section projects to a Jacobi field, and establish a converse when the corresponding base variation is contained in a single leaf of the characteristic foliation.

Geometric Topology.title: Rational knots, quivers, and tails of colored HOMFLY-PT polynomials
Geometric Topology.summary: We use the knots-quivers correspondence to prove that the colored HOMFLY-PT polynomial of a rational knot has a tail and give an explicit formula for calculating the tail in terms of the quiver.

Geometric Topology.title: On a twisted Singer conjecture
Geometric Topology.summary: According to the Singer conjecture, the $L^2$-Betti numbers of a closed aspherical manifold are expected to vanish outside the middle dimension. In this paper, we study a natural analog of the Singer conjecture concerning the vanishing of twisted $L^2$-Betti numbers outside the lower middle dimension. These invariants can be thought of as $L^2$-Betti numbers of an infinite cyclic cover, depending on a first cohomology class. This is related to a previous conjecture by the author, which connects the twisted $L^2$-Euler characteristic to the Thurston norm, and which we prove for a class of closed arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds.

Geometric Topology.summary: Let $S_g$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $g\ge2$. For a reductive representation $ρ:π_1(S_g)\to\mathrm{PU}(2,1)$, let $E_ρ$ be the energy function on Teichmüller space associated to equivariant harmonic maps into $\mathrm{CH}^2$. For every positive integer $d$ with $3\nmid d$, all sufficiently large $h$, and every $g>h$, we construct an irreducible reductive representation \[ ρ_{g,h,d}:π_1(S_g)\to\mathrm{PU}(2,1) \] with \[ τ(ρ_{g,h,d})=2h-2-\frac{2d}{3}\notin\mathbb Z, \qquad \mathrm{Crit}(E_{ρ_{g,h,d}})=\varnothing. \] Consequently, the associated branched-minimal-surface forgetful map is not surjective in these nonintegral Toledo components.

Geometric Topology.title: On Poincaré spaces which are not manifolds
Geometric Topology.summary: This expository note gives a short derivation of the classical Spivak normal fibration formula for the total space of a spherical fibration over a Poincaré duality space. We review the associated smooth, PL, and topological manifold realization criteria and illustrate them with examples from the stable stems. The principal application combines these criteria with the completed solution of the Kervaire invariant problem to identify the exceptional stems in a specified family of three cell Poincaré spaces.
Geometric Topology.comment: This paper is primarily expository. The author claims little originality for this note and does not intend to publish it in a peer-reviewed journal

Geometric Topology.title: Property $R_\infty$ for Higman$\unicode{x2013}$Thompson Groups
Geometric Topology.summary: We prove that every Higman$\unicode{x2013}$Thompson group $G_{n,r}$, with $n\ge2$ and $r\ge1$, has property $R_\infty$. In particular, every automorphism of Thompson's group $V = G_{2,1}$ has infinitely many twisted conjugacy classes. These results answer questions of Olukoya and of Lins de Araujo, de Oliveira-Tosti and Santos Rego. We also prove that a homeomorphism under which no eventually periodic sequence has a finite orbit has a locally finite centralizer in $G_{n,r}$.

Geometric Topology.title: On the monotonicity of amenable category for geometric 4-manifolds and their connected sums
Geometric Topology.summary: We show that the amenable category is monotone with respect to the domination relation for geometric $4$-manifolds and their connected sums.

Geometric Topology.title: Twisted pencils of quartics, braid monodromy factorizations, and non-Hopfian Hurwitz curves
Geometric Topology.summary: We study which groups arise as fundamental groups of complements of affine Hurwitz curves. In every such group the product of the meridians is central and maps to the vector of component degrees in homology; this rules out, for instance, the Baumslag-Solitar groups $\operatorname{BS}(p,q)$ with $\lvert p\rvert\neq\lvert q\rvert$, and the groups of links with at least two components and vanishing linking numbers. O. V. Kulikova circumvented this obstruction for $\operatorname{BS}(2,3)$ by passing to the non-Hopfian group $\operatorname{BS}(2,3)\times\mathbb{Z}$, which Vik. S. Kulikov's doubling algorithm realizes in degree $768$. We give an explicit braid monodromy factorization of degree 12 with this group. The corresponding curve is not isotopic to an algebraic curve, yet it is obtained from a union of three quartics in a pencil by a single twist along a circle. More generally, for every closed braid $\hatβ$ we realize $π_1(S^3\setminus\hatβ)\times\mathbb{Z}$ by an explicit Hurwitz curve, again a twist of a union of quartics in a pencil. In the other direction, a Hurwitz curve with group $\operatorname{BS}(k,k+1)\times\mathbb{Z}$ has degree at least $4$, as every Hurwitz curve consisting of a conic and a line is H-isotopic to an algebraic one, after separation of its critical points. Finally, we show that certain semiholomorphic germs, among them those realizing the generalized Borromean rings, are braided surfaces but not Hurwitz curve germs.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Homological Barriers to Stable Learning of First-Order Nash Equilibria
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We identify a homological barrier to stable learning of local Nash equilibria, also known as first-order Nash equilibria (FONE), in constrained non-concave differentiable games. We consider continuous deterministic learning dynamics that fix every FONE point and aim to attract all initial conditions to the full FONE set. We show that this convergence guarantee is impossible when the target set has nontrivial positive-degree cohomology, such as that arising from a loop, and the state space is compact and contractible. We exhibit this barrier in a simple non-concave quadratic zero-sum game on a box whose exact FONE set consists of a diagonal six-edge loop and an isolated point. Consequently, no such dynamics can make the full FONE set a stable global attractor. We further show that degree two is the minimal polynomial degree at which this barrier can arise and extend the construction to obtain nontrivial homology in arbitrarily high degrees. Finally, we establish that the barrier persists for sufficiently small approximate-FONE targets under small perturbations, yielding an open, positive-volume family of quadratic zero-sum games with the same homological barrier.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Competition Versus Complexity in Multiple-Selection Prophet Inequalities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Competition complexity formalizes a compelling intuition: rather than refining the mechanism, how much additional competition is sufficient for a simple mechanism to compete with an optimal one? We begin the study of this question in multi-unit pricing for welfare maximization using prophet inequalities. An online decision-maker observes $m \geq k$ nonnegative values drawn independently from a known distribution, may select up to $k$ of them, and aims to maximize the expected sum of selected values. The benchmark is a prophet who observes a sequence of length $n \geq k$ and selects the $k$ largest values. We focus on the widely adopted class of single-threshold algorithms and fully characterize their $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity. Notably, our results reveal a sharp competition-induced phase transition: in the absence of competition, single-threshold algorithms are fundamentally limited to a $1-1/\sqrt{2kπ}$ fraction of the prophet value, whereas even a $1\%$ multiplicative increase beyond $n$ observations suffices to achieve a $1-\exp(-Θ(k))$ fraction. Another notable result happens when $k=1$: we show that the $(1-\varepsilon)$-competition complexity is exactly $\ln(1/\varepsilon)$, fully resolving an open question by Brustle et al. [Math. Oper. Res. 2024]. Our analysis is based on infinite-dimensional linear programming and duality arguments.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Complexity of Computing a Competitive Equilibrium in Fisher Markets with Chores
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the complexity of computing competitive equilibria in Fisher markets with divisible chores and positive rational disutility coefficients and earning requirements. For linear disutilities, we prove that exact equilibrium computation is CLS-complete. In particular, the problem remains CLS-hard even when the earning requirements are binary in $1$ and $2^k$, where $k$ is an integer. We prove hardness by encoding the first-order conditions of a box-constrained quadratic program in equilibrium prices and earning flows, using a compact minimum-cost flow construction. For convex constant-elasticity-of-substitution (CES) disutilities, exact equilibrium prices may be irrational. We formulate the problem of finite-precision equilibrium price computation, in which we seek rational prices with a certified market clearing error at most a given rational tolerance encoded in binary. We prove that this problem is CLS-complete for every fixed rational exponent $ρ>1$. To prove this hardness, we encode a quartic polynomial through the fourth-order expansion of the CES price potential function corresponding to the Eisenberg-Gale (EG) dual program, and show that every sufficiently accurate approximate equilibrium of the constructed market lies near uniform prices. Additionally, we also identify a tractable special case of chores Fisher markets. In particular, we provide a strongly polynomial algorithm for exact equilibrium computation in linear markets whose disutility matrix has rank at most two and earning requirements are arbitrary positive rationals. For $n$ agents and $m$ chores, the algorithm uses $O(nm(n+m))$ rational arithmetic operations and comparisons, with polynomial intermediate encoding length.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Large-Market Discipline in Combinatorial Double Auctions: No Recombination, Bundle Selection, and Complementarities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Licences can forbid assembling bundles from several sellers or splitting them among buyers, a restriction we call No Recombination. We study its welfare cost in a double auction as the number of traders on each side of the market grows. We ask whether that cost vanishes as a share of welfare, as the gain from misreporting does with a single good. With two goods and Gaussian shocks, consider the prices that would prevail under free recombination. As the market grows, the loss as a share of optimal welfare vanishes if and only if expected demand for the two-good bundle equals expected supply of whole bundles at those prices. Otherwise the loss persists. In our market, sellers can never gain by misreporting. With two goods, buyers who commit to bidding their values plus fixed margins misreport in symmetric equilibria by amounts that vanish as the market grows. Under these conditions, in large markets No Recombination outweighs strategic bidding as a source of loss.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 107 pages, including a 55-page online appendix

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Complexity of Strong Popularity in Hedonic Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
In a hedonic game, agents are partitioned into coalitions and have preferences over the coalitions they may join. A partition is called strongly popular if it strictly beats every other partition in a majority vote among the agents.
  We study the complexity of determining the existence of strongly popular partitions in two fundamental classes of hedonic games: additively separable and fractional hedonic games (ASHGs and FHGs), where agents' utilities are determined, respectively, by the sum and average of their valuations for the members of their coalitions.
  We prove that this problem is PCW-complete for ASHGs and for FHGs even with non-negative valuations, where PCW is a subclass of $Σ^P_2$ associated with unambiguous problems (which have at most one witness), recently introduced by Gilboa et al. (2025). These are the first natural complete problems for PCW, in the sense that their formulations do not involve arbitrary Boolean circuits. Our results resolve open problems posed by Brandt and Bullinger (JAIR 2022) and Bullinger and Gilboa (IJCAI 2025). The two reductions employ substantially different techniques, reflecting both the distinct utility models and the stringent non-negativity constraint in FHGs.
  Furthermore, in contrast with FHGs, we show that in ASHGs restricting valuations to be non-negative makes the problem polynomial-time solvable.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: This version includes additional results: Theorems 1.2 and 1.3. A preliminary version of Theorem 1.1 in this paper appeared as part of earlier versions of arXiv:2510.19084, when the two works formed a single manuscript

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Welfare in Envy-free Contracts: When Agents Have Sparse Interests
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study welfare maximization under envy-free contracts, where a principal assigns tasks and offers success-contingent payments to heterogeneous agents with hidden effort. For unit-demand agents, we establish a sharp complexity boundary: the problem is polynomial-time solvable when each agent is interested in at most two tasks, but NP-hard with at most three interests. Our algorithm analyzes tree-structured dependencies among forced assignments and reduces optimization to maximum-weight independent set in a perfect graph. When agents may receive multiple tasks, no polynomial-time constant-factor approximation exists unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. Finally, with homogeneous success probabilities and rewards, we establish a welfare- and revenue-preserving equivalence between unit-demand contract design and envy-free pricing. This yields polynomial-time welfare maximization without restricting interests, while revenue maximization remains NP-hard.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Power of Menus in Dynamic Pricing: Optimal Regret and Equivalence Results
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study dynamic pricing where a seller repeatedly interacts with a strategic, non-myopic buyer who has a fixed private valuation and discounts future utility. Prior work focused exclusively on posted-price mechanisms, where the seller gives a take-it-or-leave-it offer. For our first result, under geometric discounting $γ_t = γ^{t-1}$, we show that menu mechanisms consisting of allocation-payment contracts achieve $O(T_γ)$ regret, where $T_γ$ is the buyer's effective discounted time horizon. We also establish a $Ω(T_γ)$ lower bound, demonstrating the bound is tight. Considering the geometric discounting buyer with a constant discount factor, our bound is $O(1)$, while prior bounds using posted-price mechanisms incur an unavoidable $Ω(\log\log T)$ factor in regret. Our second contribution is more conceptual in nature. The problem of dynamic pricing sits at the intersection of two paradigms: learning with strategic agents in computer science / machine learning and revelation-principle-based mechanism design in economics, yet their relationship has remained unclear. We establish an equivalence between these two classes of mechanisms in our single-buyer setting: any adaptive indirect menu mechanism can be converted into an incentive-compatible direct mechanism with no less revenue, and conversely, any such direct mechanism can be implemented by an adaptive indirect menu mechanism with no less revenue. Consequently, the two classes achieve identical optimal regret. The adaptive, data-driven algorithms of online learning and explicit type elicitation from direct revelation type mechanisms are two languages towards solving the same problem.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Welfare, Improvability, and Variance: A Principal-Agent Approach to Optimal Benchmark Item Aggregation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: AI benchmarks have well-documented limitations, with prior work examining contamination, saturation, and construct underspecification. Aggregation has received far less attention: benchmarks are typically summarized by uniformly averaging item-level scores, implicitly treating every test item as equally valuable. We model benchmarking as a multitask principal-agent game and show that the welfare loss from a benchmark is determined jointly by three item-level primitives: alignment with normative welfare priorities, marginal improvability, and performance variance. We translate the theory into an audit framework that ranks items along each of these three axes, and apply it to OLMES items using WORKBank for welfare, the EvoLM 4B suite for improvability, and the PolyPythias 410M panel for variance. The framework surfaces items that are Pareto-inferior within OLMES subject to a pro-worker welfare operationalization. All code is available at https://github.com/stair-lab/principal-agent-benchmarks.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS'26 Evaluations & Datasets Track

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Distributed Learning of $α$-Potential Functions in Strategic Multi-agent Systems
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the problem of computing the tightest \(α\)-potential approximation of a general-sum game over continuous action spaces, within a prescribed class of potential functions and when each player has access only to its own utility function. The difficulty is twofold: the approximation error involves a worst-case search over an infinite set of unilateral deviations, and the required utility information is distributed across players.
  For a linear-in-parameters potential class, we use an exact finite-tuple reformulation that separates the problem into a global outer search over deviation tuples and distributed convex inner problems. We develop a primal--dual inner oracle tailored to this structure and establish a uniform one-sided accuracy guarantee. This oracle can be combined with global outer search to obtain an end-to-end guarantee on the outer optimization error. We also develop a projected zeroth-order outer method as a computationally lighter alternative for higher-dimensional problems. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy--computation tradeoff between the two outer-search methods and show that the proposed optimization framework can improve upon analytical \(α\)-potential constructions.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Finite-Sample and Communication-Efficient Networked Information Aggregation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Building on SODA 2026 work Kearns et al. (2026), we study learning in directed acyclic graphs in which each agent observes only a subset of the input coordinates and may use the predictions of its parents as additional features. In the finite-sample protocol, the message sent along each edge is the agent's prediction vector on a shared sample, so the communication cost is linear in the sample size $m$. In this paper we study this model under communication constraints.
  First, we revisit the finite-sample analysis of the full-message protocol. We identify a gap in the finite-sample proof of Kearns et al. (2026) and develop a different argument that establishes a finite-sample population-risk guarantee along paths satisfying deterministic $M$-coverage.
  Second, we introduce a shared-sketch protocol in which each agent sends a $k$-dimensional linear sketch of its prediction vector instead of the full $m$-dimensional message, where $k\ll m$. We analyze this protocol through a reduction to least squares on the compressed sample together with an oblivious subspace embedding argument. The resulting bound separates statistics from communication: the statistical term is still governed by the original sample size $m$, while the additional error due to compression is controlled by the sketch dimension $k$. For Gaussian sketches, we obtain an explicit high-probability population-risk bound, showing that row subsampling is not the only possible communication-statistics tradeoff for networked information aggregation.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Exploring Mixed-Reality for Enhancing Driver Warning Systems: A Preliminary Study on Attention-Shifting Methods and Hazard Perception
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Modern vehicles are equipped with advanced sensors and capabilities, yet engaging human drivers effectively in hazard perception remains a challenging research area. This paper investigates the potential of mixed reality (MR) to enhance driver warning systems. The study examines the impact of attention-shifting methods, including visual cues, audio cues, and a combination of both, on drivers' hazard perception. A preliminary study involving six participants was conducted, and the NASA-TLX analysis did not yield significant differences. However, through the use of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), we unveil distinct brain activation patterns associated with visual and sound cues. Further research with larger sample sizes and diverse driving scenarios is required to validate and expand upon these preliminary results.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Feel My Focus: Gaze-Triggered Digital Twin Creation for Remote Collaboration
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We present Feel My Focus, a gaze-triggered mixed reality (MR) demonstration that enables rapid creation and sharing of lightweight 3D digital twins during remote collaboration. Unlike systems that use gaze primarily as a referential pointer, Feel My Focus treats sustained visual attention as a generative action: a fixation on a physical object initiates single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation, and one-shot 3D reconstruction, allowing a remote partner to inspect and discuss the object in situ. The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and an MR client for runtime streaming and interaction. This design prioritizes responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity. We report observations from a public demonstration, highlighting design trade-offs, failure modes, and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults. However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures. This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case. XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment). However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified. The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning. Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component. Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Review article. 22 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables; Supplementary Materials (19 pages); ancillary files: the Supplementary Materials (PDF), File S1 (evidence map, XLSX and CSV) and File S2 (XR inventory, XLSX)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Sketch to Design: A Cross-scale Workflow for Procedural Generative Urban Design
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Urban designers use sketches and symbols to express spatial intentions, while many generative urban design tools rely on numeric parameters that are difficult to relate to this visual process. We propose a cross-scale workflow and a web-based prototype that translates symbolic sketches into controllable procedural urban generation. A vocabulary of shapes, informed by examples of urban design diagrams and sketching exercises with graduate urban design students, encodes attributes such as network structure, density, and program. The prototype uses the \$1 Unistroke Recognizer to map gestures to symbols and translates their locations and sizes into tensor-field attractors and weighted parameter grids. Grid and radial tensor fields guide street-network generation, while the parameter grids control building heights and programs. Implemented in JavaScript and TypeScript with React and Three.js, the prototype supports interactive sketching, visualization, and urban massing generation. We describe the methodology and illustrate prototype interactions, then discuss downstream integration with architectural-scale generative tools for further refinement and analysis. The work connects designers' symbolic input with an explicit procedural generation process.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 7 pages, 6 figures. Author version of a paper published at CAADRIA 2024

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Dashboard Remixing: Goal-oriented Organization and Enrichment of Visualizations and Insights
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Dashboard creation requires iteratively authoring multiple views and organizing them into a structured format. However, creators often struggle to step back and assess their own work for organization and refinement due to cognitive limitations. In this work, we propose a pipeline to provide computational support for self-reflection during the design process. Our pipeline automatically infers analytical objectives, discovers implicit patterns, and structures those patterns to surface coherent analytical pathways. It further enriches existing dashboard designs by generating complementary visualizations and aggregating natural language insights based on relationships across data entities (e.g., contrasting, drill-down, and relatedness) to reveal chart connections. Our rule-based pipeline provides objective, verifiable feedback, offering an external perspective while enabling creators to tell their own data stories. Four case studies and six expert interviews demonstrate how this approach helps creators reflect on organizational alternatives and surface hidden analytical opportunities in a principled way, reducing the cognitive burden while encouraging deeper analytical exploration.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From MNH to the Friedman--Komogortsev Method---which changes improve eye-movement classification?
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The Friedman-Komogortsev Method (FKM) is a rule-based classifier of fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations in 1000-Hz recordings, developed from the modified Nyström-Holmqvist algorithm (MNH) and used in several recent studies. FKM changes MNH in many ways at once: it centres MNH's Savitzky-Golay filter, adds a position-based test for whether an apparent post-saccadic oscillation continues the saccade, adds rejection tests, and changes several thresholds. We asked which of these changes alter agreement with human classification. Both algorithms were scored against twenty 26-s GazeBase reading recordings hand-classified by three trained raters, and each change was reverted in turn. FKM agreed better than MNH as MNH was used: saccade Cohen's kappa rose on all 20 recordings (median +0.034), and saccade boundaries moved from 2-3 ms late to the raters' sample. One change produced this: centring the filter, which removes a three-sample delay. Reinstating the delay returned FKM's saccade kappa to MNH's value, and centring MNH's filter alone made MNH match FKM on saccades and exceed it on post-saccadic events. The position-based test changed how saccades with several velocity peaks were divided, splitting 8% of rater-labelled "wavy" saccades into a saccade and a spurious oscillation against 39% for delay-corrected MNH. FKM's higher post-saccadic velocity floor traded recall for precision. The remaining changes had no measurable effect on these recordings. FKM's improvement over MNH is therefore a filter-alignment correction that MNH users can apply directly, plus a segmentation rule for multi-peak saccades.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: The details about the classification is described in the supplementary materials

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Facilitating the Integration of LLMs Into Online Experiments With Simple Chat
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly prevalent, understanding human-LLM interactions is emerging as a central priority in psychological research. Online experiments offer an efficient means to study human-LLM interactions, yet integrating LLMs into established survey platforms remains technically demanding, particularly when aiming for ecologically realistic, real-time conversational experiences with strong experimental control. We introduce Simple Chat, an open-source, research-focused chat interface that streamlines LLM integration for platforms such as Qualtrics, oTree, and LimeSurvey, while presenting a unified participant experience across conditions. Simple Chat connects to both commercial providers and open-weights models, displays streamed responses incrementally, and offers an administrative interface for fine-grained control of prompts and interface features. Simple Chat is available both as a hosted service that requires no installation and as open-source software that researchers can deploy on their own server or adapt to their needs. By reducing technical barriers and standardizing interfaces, Simple Chat helps advance the study of human-LLM interaction. In this article, we outline Simple Chat's key features, provide a step-by-step tutorial, and demonstrate its utility through two illustrative case studies.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Revised version

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Dialogue to Task: How Cognitive Engagement With Generative Artificial Intelligence Relates to Post-Dialogue Activity and Task Outcomes
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative AI is increasingly embedded within learning tasks, yet interaction frequency reveals little about cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue. Little is known about how such engagement is situated within task workflows or how dialogue characteristics and subsequent task activity relate to students' behaviour and task outcomes. This study examined cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue, its position within task workflows, and associations of dialogue and task-process characteristics with post-dialogue activity and task outcomes. Data were collected from 1,681 students across 40 university courses using three AI companions embedded in resource creation, peer moderation, and practice. Cognitive engagement in 829 conversation threads was coded with a dialogue-oriented Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework, and 2,969 task sequences were modelled with first-order Markov models. Regression models linked dialogue and task-process characteristics to behavioural re-engagement, peer-rated artefact quality, and practice performance. Passive and Active engagement predominated, although resource creation involved more Constructive and Interactive dialogue, peer moderation more Passive, and practice more Active, while higher-engagement dialogue was less often followed by session termination. In resource creation, student-composed messages were associated with more dialogue-to-task returns than template-only requests at the same Passive level, whereas deeper cognitive engagement was associated with higher final artefact quality independent of return frequency; in practice, AI dialogue after an incorrect attempt was associated with fewer further attempts but higher next-attempt correctness among continuers. Post-dialogue activity and task outcomes are distinct aspects of AI use that interaction frequency cannot capture and evaluations should assess separately.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 31 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Computer Assisted Learning

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Linking Event-sequence Data Claims to Analytic Provenance in Chatbots: Technique and Evaluation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Chatbots are increasingly used to analyze temporal event sequences of which website clickstreams are among the most common. Explanations are essential for understanding claims about event-sequence data. However, existing systems often require programming expertise to interpret these explanations and fail to explain the data processes underlying the data claims. We introduce a technique for linking a data claim to its analytic provenance (i.e., the analytic steps and results that produced it). It has two components: a reference table that records analytic steps and results in addressable cells, and a citation format that binds each claim to one or more cells. To operationalize this technique for clickstream analysis, we curated a set of analytic operations for clickstream analysis, organized them through a pivot-table abstraction, and developed tools that an AI agent can invoke to create a reference table and assemble a natural language response with cited data claims. To evaluate how citations affect users' assessment of data claims, we conducted two crowdsourced experiments with 90 participants each. The experiments showed that participants perceived correct data claims to be more accurate with citations when compared with no explanations, and that they perceived incorrect data claims to be less accurate with citations when compared with code and no explanations.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation (CRAFT), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (PACM IMWUT), Vol. 10, No. 3, Article 81, September 2026. This research was supported in part by the CityU Start-up Grant (No. 9610677) and the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong under the Early Career Scheme (Project No. 24612523)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Who Benefits from Wikipedia's Growth Mentorship? The Role of Newcomer Information Needs
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Evaluations of Wikipedia's programs for new editors usually ask whether a program works on average; we ask which newcomers benefit when their question to a mentor gets a reply. English Wikipedia's Growth mentorship system assigns every new account a volunteer mentor, and about a quarter of the questions newcomers send never get a reply. Using the first questions of 34,073 newcomers (2021 to 2026), we compare newcomers who received a reply with similar newcomers who did not, matched on 164 characteristics recorded before the question (propensity score stratification). (1) Does a reply help newcomers keep editing? Yes, in the short term: in the 14 days after the reply, newcomers who received one were 1.8 percentage points (pp) more likely to edit an article (22% vs. an estimated 20% without a reply) and 1.8pp more likely to edit on two or more days. Later in the first year, the only difference that remains significant after correction for multiple testing is in the share who edit an article at least once between six months and one year after the reply (+1.5pp). (2) Does the effect depend on what the newcomer asked? Yes. We sort questions by Morrison's (1993) information-seeking types, which earlier studies measured mostly through self-reports, using a language model checked against human labels. A reply has significant effects for questions about rules and norms (+3.4pp), questions that show the newcomer's earlier editing (+3.4pp) and specific how-to questions (+2.4pp). For newcomers who do not know what to work on, a reply has no detectable effect, and the effect is 4.2pp smaller than for newcomers with other questions. (3) Which replies are followed by more editing? Among newcomers who received a reply, those whose reply came sooner or stayed closer to the topic of their question edited more.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 25 pages, 10 figures. Accepted at ICWSM 2027

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Wording Matters: Understanding How GenAI Policy Rules Shape Teachers' and Students' Workflows and Perceptions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The growing use of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education has led institutions to develop policies governing its applications. However, we have little knowledge about how teachers and students adapt and adhere to the policies. In this paper, we analyzed GenAI policies from 101 U.S. universities, identifying nine recurring rules for GenAI use, and interviewed 20 students and 20 faculty members about the rules. We find that the wording of the rules can change how students perceive and act on the rules while introducing different challenges that teachers face in enforcing them in practice. For example, rules such as "Passing off AI-generated content as your own constitutes academic dishonesty" and "Students are accountable for any inaccurate, biased, or unethical content" both outline the acceptable use of AI, but the former can make students hide their use of AI out of fear of unwanted scrutiny, whereas the latter can encourage students to take responsibility and ownership of their use of AI and be more transparent. Students described uncertainty about acceptable use, fear of penalties and unfair treatment, and stigma that discouraged acknowledging AI use. Teachers took on approval workload, had to interpret acceptable use, and lacked reliable ways to verify compliance. We summarize these impacts in a policy-impact matrix linking each rule to its effects on teacher and student workflows and perception.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: GARP: Real-Time Generative Agents on Local Hardware in a Game Engine
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative agents are game characters whose plans, conversations, and memories are written on the fly by a large language model (LLM). The original Generative Agents demonstration used cloud inference in a custom simulation. We present GARP, a platform for real-time generative agents inside Godot, and describe the Character Behavior System used in GARP 2. The complete loop runs on local hardware using a 3B-parameter open-weight model and no cloud service. Alongside the original planning, memory, and reflection, GARP gives each agent an emotion system driven by LLM appraisal, four graded personality axes drawn from the Big Five that set simulation parameters as well as prompt text, six needs whose urgency grows over time, and pairwise relationships updated after every conversation. The system narrows 50+ candidate actions to typically 3-8, constrains model responses with JSON schemas, and surfaces important memories in decision prompts. A layered optimization strategy (an adjustable game clock, decisions taken ahead of need, multi-tier caching, prompt compression, and fully asynchronous execution) keeps the game responsive while the model thinks. In a nine-scenario evaluation, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks. Both failures occurred in the birthday party scenario, where one guest omitted the event from their daily plan.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 13 pages, 13 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Known Good, Known Bad: A Ground-Truth Calibration Protocol for AI Judgment in Science
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Scientific use of generative AI requires evaluation against cases with independently checkable answers. We present a ground truth calibration protocol that compares a verified reference case with reference deviant variants through neutral evaluation, an authority framed recheck, and a line by line audit. Human adjudication distinguishes deviation detection, premise accommodation, unsupported doubt, and correctness of the resulting calculation.
  An instructor generated organic chemistry demonstration comprises six conversations and 18 responses from an unidentified backend served through the free logged out ChatGPT interface in July 2026. Neutral evaluation detected three of five intended deviations. Both initial misses, involving oxidant stoichiometry and experimental scale, were detected at the authority framed second turn; all five detections persisted at the third turn audit. The fixed sequence supports a descriptive account of recovery across turns. In the scale case, the model initially produced a locally coherent peroxide limited yield. After recognizing the unit problem, it incorrectly retained that limiting reagent conclusion for the corrected scale. Detection and numerical repair therefore require separate assessment. The verified reference attracted speculative concerns while retaining its correct yield calculation.
  The protocol connects documentary verification of scientific claims and citations with empirical verification of laboratory interpretations. It supplies inspectable transcripts, reference calculations, behavior codes, and a reusable calibration architecture for AI literacy instruction. The pilot demonstrates the protocol's measures in one case family; replicated model evaluation and learner assessment are the next validation steps.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Boule or Baguette? A Study on Task Topology, Length Generalization, and the Benefit of Reasoning Traces
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Recent years have witnessed meteoric progress in reasoning models: neural networks that generate intermediate reasoning traces (RTs) before producing a final output. Despite the rapid advancement, our understanding of how RTs support reasoning, and where this paradigm fails, remain incomplete. To promote greater clarity, we introduce PITA: a novel large-scale dataset of over 23 million statements in propositional logic and their corresponding proofs. As a benchmark for robust reasoning, we focus on length generalization: if a model is trained to determine truth or falsity on statements with proofs up to fixed length, how well does it generalize to statements requiring longer proofs? We propose notions of (1) task depth and (2) task breadth, which measure respectively (1) the number of proof steps required to solve a proposition and (2) the number of unique propositions within a task family. We vary these quantities across subsets of PITA, and find that RT models generalize well on relatively broad and shallow subsets, while deteriorating on relatively narrow and deep subsets compared to non-RT baselines. As a controlled point of comparison, we study a separate, tractable transitive inference task that exhibits qualitatively similar behavior. Our accompanying theory explains the scalings observed in this simpler setting, suggesting one mechanism by which breadth can favor RT models while depth can expose long-context weaknesses. Our findings suggest salient benefits and limitations of proof-like reasoning traces in controlled length-generalization settings.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: Published at NeurIPS 2026. 51 pages, 12 figures, code available at https://github.com/wtong98/boule-or-baguette

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Understanding Spike Encoding across IoT Sensing Modalities: An Empirical Study
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a path to energy-efficient sensing on Internet of Things (IoT) devices. The input encoder shapes that opportunity by changing the cues available for recognition and the work required to process them. We study these choices across wireless, inertial, surface electromyographic, and tactile sensing. For wireless activity recognition, interleaving reduces estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers, latency from the prepared input window to returned scores, and energy on the graphics processing unit and system-on-chip (GPU/SoC) rail, compared with repeating the full window on Jetson AGX Orin. With the same input size at each SNN time step, repeating a compact input can yield higher mean development accuracy than interleaving. The inertial experiments show that higher accuracy can come at higher device cost. Direct input can also be faster and more accurate than an event encoder while using less energy on the measured rail, even when its estimated energy for arithmetic in the network layers is higher. Level crossings improve grasp recognition on a later day for previously observed users. In tactile slip detection, level crossings shift the balance between missed slips and false alarms, and checkpoint selection can reverse which input offers higher slip recall. We use these findings to outline how edge sensing systems can profile encoders against the signal structure, the errors that matter to the task, and the cost of the full inference pipeline.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables; includes supplementary material

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: From Search to Signal: Search-Value Credit for Evolutionary Automatic Heuristic Design
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Large language models generate candidate programs for automatic heuristic design, while evolutionary search evaluates and selects them to guide further generation. Online post-training uses rewards from candidate evaluations to adapt the generator. Retained programs can also guide later generation as parents. This motivates rewards that reflect their reuse opportunities beyond immediate fitness. We propose Search-value credit (SVC), which constructs response-level rewards from actual admission to the retained set and a short-term parent-exposure proxy. Admission determines reward eligibility; the proxy weights eligible responses by reuse opportunities under existing parent-selection rules. Rewards are computed after candidate evaluation, without evaluating descendants. SVC retains the search and learning procedures of the Co-Evolution of Algorithms and Language Model (CALM) framework. Across four combinatorial optimization tasks with the same base model and response budget, SVC achieves the best mean final search performance on three tasks among six conditions. Under identical prompts and parents on traveling salesman and capacitated vehicle routing tasks, SVC-trained generators yield a higher mean proportion of responses whose programs outperform the best prompting parent than those trained with CALM's native reward. These findings support reward construction using search retention and selection information.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 80 pages, including supplementary material. Substantially revised version introducing Search-Value Credit (SVC), with a redesigned reward mechanism and expanded experiments

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Neural Activity Synchronization-Based Fast Local Learnable Spiking Neural Network Architecture
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Implementing intelligent learning systems on low- power edge devices is challenging due to the high compu- tational complexity, training latency, and energy demands of traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), biologically plausible and spike-driven, come as an alternative. However, SNN training commonly relies on backpropagation through time (BPTT), which is computationally expensive, inherently global, and unsuitable for battery-driven devices. This work proposes a novel local learning framework for multi-layered SNNs inspired by Neural Activity Synchronization (NAS). Each layer updates its own weights using locally com- puted gradients. No gradient backpropagation is needed. This significantly reduces computational complexity, training latency, and energy consumption. The proposed SNN model is trained and evaluated on the MNIST dataset, achieving a classification accuracy of 97.78%. The model is also analyzed with Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, demonstrating robust performance across different noise levels.

Methodology.title: Comparing randomized trials: a formal approach
Methodology.summary: Disagreements between randomized trials that address the same causal question pose challenges for the interpretation and synthesis of evidence. We sketch a causal framework for comparing the results of randomized trials that explicitly accommodates the possibility of trial engagement effects. Using counterfactual outcomes defined under joint interventions on treatment assignment and trial-related actions, we compare trial-native treatment effects with the effects transported from one trial to the population of another in a common target population. We show that standard conditions for transporting treatment effects across trial populations are not sufficient to guarantee agreement between transported and trial-native effects. Agreement additionally requires conditions governing how trial-related actions affect outcome across studies - for example, absence of trial engagement effects, equivalence of such effects across trials, or lack of interaction between trial engagement and treatment assignment. Our framework clarifies potential sources of disagreement across trials and extends existing approaches to study comparison to settings in which trial engagement effects may be present.

Methodology.title: ATHOS: Agreement-based Testing of Hypotheses in Overlapping Subgroups
Methodology.summary: We study confirmation of treatment benefit in a prespecified family of overlapping subgroups of a randomized trial. Maximum-statistic procedures exploit the correlation between subgroups' statistics, but calibration decides what they protect. Re-randomization controls error exactly when treatment has no effect, but not when only an average effect is zero, whereas a multiplier bootstrap protects average effects only asymptotically. Our first result characterizes when re-randomization alone protects average effects. It reverses the arms' weights in the statistics' covariance, so with unequal allocation and heterogeneous effects it can overstate their correlations; in one such family of 50 subgroups, its limiting familywise error is 0.064 at nominal 0.025. We propose a step-down procedure called ATHOS, short for agreement-based testing of hypotheses in overlapping subgroups, which confirms a subgroup only when both calibrations reject it. Given assignments exchangeable within strata, ATHOS controls familywise error exactly when treatment has no effect and, under complete randomization, asymptotically for average effects, even in large families. Our second result shows that requiring agreement costs no first-order local power in balanced trials. In a null simulation with 200 patients and 1,497 subgroups, the bootstrap step-down alone made false claims in 40% of trials and ATHOS in 2.6%. In two comparisons in an HIV trial, ATHOS confirmed 188 and 73 subgroups and Holm's procedure 179 and 62.

Methodology.title: Nonasymptotic causal structure learning in generalized linear DAGs with continuous optimization
Methodology.summary: We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

Methodology.title: Graph Fourier Neural Kernels: Learning Full PDE Trajectories Across Geometries and Anisotropic Parameter Fields
Methodology.summary: High-fidelity simulations of time-dependent nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) are expensive to repeat across families of domains and parameter fields, a cost that recurs in design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and computational medicine. Most neural-operator surrogates require each domain to be mapped onto a common grid or reference shape, and few predict the full time course. We introduce Graph Fourier Neural Kernels (G-FuNK), a neural operator for second-order semilinear PDEs with a diffusive principal part that transfers across geometries and anisotropic diffusion tensors without coordinate maps or diffeomorphisms. A weighted graph and its Laplacian supply a spectral basis that encodes geometry and anisotropy. Shared layers act in this basis, at a cost linear in mesh size after one partial eigendecomposition per geometry, and a neural ODE integrator propagates the learned generator to full spatiotemporal trajectories on unseen domains. Across anisotropic heat flow, stiff reaction-diffusion, FitzHugh-Nagumo, and patient-specific left-atrial electrophysiology on CT-derived surfaces, G-FuNK reproduces held-out trajectories with relative $L^2$ error between 0.046 and 0.160. Its accuracy is comparable to that of a geometry-aware Fourier neural operator on regular domains, and its predictions are unchanged when a rectangular domain is rotated. On left atria, whose venous and valvular openings prevent mapping onto a reference shape, it predicts an 85-ms trajectory in under half a second, against about 5 minutes for finite elements, with a mean activation-time error of 1.73 ms. Accuracy depends on graph construction and is highest when the learned generator is integrated at its training time step.

Methodology.title: Toward a Unified Statistical Theory of Multi-View Pretraining for Neural Knowledge Graph Learning
Methodology.summary: Knowledge graph learning offers a powerful framework for representing and inferring structured knowledge, with broad practical applications. Two obstacles limit current methods: labeled triples are scarce for each entity and relation, which makes expressive models hard to train, and scoring functions are designed ad hoc, which limits their generalizability and leaves them without theoretical grounding. We address both obstacles with a theoretically grounded framework, with end-to-end guarantees, that extends and subsumes existing methods. The framework proceeds in two stages: multi-view unsupervised pretraining that integrates heterogeneous sources of entity side information into a shared representation, followed by supervised learning across multiple relation types. We establish a unified nonasymptotic risk bound that combines the subspace recovery error of pretraining and the sample complexity of the labeled data in a single guarantee, quantifying formally how large-scale unlabeled data from multiple views benefits downstream knowledge prediction. Synthetic experiments validate each component of the theory, and experiments on large-scale real-world knowledge graph benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our approach.
Methodology.comment: 37 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. To appear in the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Methodology.title: Express Language Modeling
Methodology.summary: We introduce a new tool, Express, for converting a non-causal attention approximation into a causal approximation with matching approximation guarantees. When combined with the state-of-the-art Thinformer approximation, Express improves upon the best known causal attention guarantees, delivering $\log^{3/2}(n)/s$ approximation error with only $O(s)$ memory and $O(s^2 \log^2(n))$ compression overhead for a sequence of length $n$. We pair these developments with an efficient I/O-aware Triton implementation, demonstrate substantial speedups over FlashAttention 2, and use Express to overcome four resource bottlenecks in the language modeling pipeline: long-context prefill, KV cache compression, long-form memory-constrained decoding, and long-form compute-constrained decoding.

Methodology.title: Personalized Pricing with Invalid Instrumental Variables: Identification, Estimation, and Policy Learning
Methodology.summary: Pricing based on individual customer characteristics is widely used to maximize sellers' revenues. We study how a firm can learn such a personalized pricing policy from historical transactions when unobserved factors affect both the prices it charged and the revenue it earned. Standard instrumental variable (IV) methods either focus on a discrete treatment space or require that the IV affect revenue only through price. This exclusion restriction is difficult to justify in pricing, where the most natural candidate IVs are price-setting levers that may also affect revenue directly. We propose PRINT (Personalized pRicing using Invalid iNsTrumental variables), a policy learning method for continuous prices that uses such candidate IVs. Relying on structural models of revenue and price, we show that the optimal pricing policy can be identified with invalid IV that shifts higher moments of historical prices, when the unobserved factors that drive customers' price sensitivity are separated from those used by the historical pricing rule. Based on this identification, which leads to conditional moment restrictions with generalized residual functions, we construct an adversarial min-max estimator that accommodates flexible machine learning models and establish regret bounds for the learned pricing policy. Simulation studies and an application to a U.S. online auto lender illustrate the method's performance. Our results give a principled way to learn personalized prices from observational data using imperfect price-setting levers, and clarify when doing so is justified.

Methodology.title: A Bayesian approach to the survivor average causal effect in cluster-randomized crossover trials
Methodology.summary: In cluster-randomized crossover (CRXO) trials, groups of individuals are randomly assigned to one of two or more sequences of alternating treatments. Since clusters serve as their own control, the CRXO design is typically more statistically efficient than the usual parallel-arm design. CRXO trials are increasingly popular in many areas of health research where the number of available clusters is limited. Further, in trials among severely ill patients, researchers often want to assess the effect of treatments on secondary non-terminal outcomes, but frequently in these studies, there are patients who do not survive to have these measurements fully recorded. In this paper, we provide a causal inference framework and treatment effect estimation method for addressing truncation by death in the setting of CRXO trials. We target the survivor average causal effect (SACE) estimand, a well-defined subgroup treatment effect obtained via principal stratification. We propose causal structural assumptions and standard parametric modeling assumptions that together enable estimating the SACE within a Bayesian paradigm. We evaluate the small-sample performance of our proposed Bayesian approach for estimation of the SACE in CRXO trial settings via simulation studies. We apply our method to a previously conducted two-period cross-sectional CRXO study examining the impact of proton pump inhibitors compared to histamine-2 receptor blockers on length of hospitalization among adults requiring invasive mechanical ventilation.
Methodology.comment: Revisions for clarity of assumptions and methods. Expansion of appendix, including addition of assumptions for stepped-wedge trials. New authorship

Methodology.title: Graph-regularized synthetic control for spatial panels with post-only treated locations
Methodology.summary: Spatial policy panels can contain treated locations that are observed only after an intervention and therefore have no pre-treatment outcome history. Without a pre-treatment trajectory to match, choosing donor weights for such post-only locations requires an additional source of information. We propose Graph-SCM, which estimates donor weights jointly across treated locations and encourages geographically neighboring locations to use similar donor combinations.
