Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The objective of this study is to demonstrate the potential of generating context-aware eco-feedback - eco-feedback that reflects a household's contextual characteristics alongside its energy use patterns - through a large language model-integrated framework. Previous studies have introduced personalized eco-feedback, mostly relying on household energy use patterns; however, they frequently did not reflect distinct household characteristics, including their persona or non-negotiable routines, leaving eco-feedback ineffective and sometimes superficial. To address these limitations, we introduce a contextual engineering framework that generates eco-feedback using a self-consistency with chain-of-thought prompt, leveraging household energy analysis data, utility rate structures, and household characteristic information. We conducted a rigorous empirical validation and a combinatorial evaluation analysis to assess this framework systematically. The former tested the framework's ability to generate accurate and contextually grounded eco-feedback for three households by comparing its output against reference interventions independently derived from the same household data. The latter examined the framework's adaptability across 400 scenarios spanning 50 households, two utility rate structures, and four behavioral personas. Our framework generated eco-feedback that aligned with reference interventions at a mean rate of 92.0% and grounded its recommendations in the provided household data with 95.7% citation accuracy. It also proved highly adaptive, shifting both the appliances targeted and the energy-saving strategies recommended in response to rate structure and household context. Ultimately, this study contributes to realizing the next level of context-aware interactions between occupants and buildings which paves the way for higher occupant living quality and sustainability.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 33 pages, 12 figures, 12 tables. Accepted manuscript. The peer-reviewed and published version appears in Energy and Buildings 370 (2026) 118038. Re-set in the HUBS Lab paper layout (HUBS Lab Paper No. 2026-003); content unchanged

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Computational Raga Recognition: A Theory-Driven Approach
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Raga recognition in Hindustani classical music is difficult because a raga is not defined only by the notes used in it. Its identity also depends on the way notes are emphasized, the movement between notes and characteristic phrases. In this work, we develop a computational approach to analyse these characteristics directly from audio recordings. The method uses pitch extracted from recordings and represents it using a 44-position note framework based on the 22-shruti system. From this representation, Raga features based on the Indian classical musicology are extracted.Each feature is compared with a reference representation of the raga and the resulting scores are combined to obtain an overall similarity score. The method is first studied using Raga Yaman and is then tested on recordings of other ragas. The computational results are also compared with the theoretical description of Yaman to identify which raga characteristics are captured well and where the method has limitations.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 16 pages, 6 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Alignment De-Identifies Without Aligning: A Congruence-Invariant Relational Gap in Cross-Subject Neural Representations
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: In brain-computer interfaces, inter-subject variability remains a major challenge that limits decoding performance across users. Subject-wise alignment is widely used to improve cross-subject transfer of neural decoders, yet it is typically evaluated only through decoding accuracy, which cannot determine whether aligned representations share greater task-related structure. We therefore distinguish two questions that accuracy conflates: whether alignment removes subject-specific information and whether it makes the relational organization of task conditions more similar across individuals. Using three motor imagery-EEG cohorts, trials are represented as covariance matrices and aligned by recentering each subject's mean covariance to a common reference. Subject-specific information is quantified with a subject-identification probe, whereas relational structure is assessed using representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) computed from condition means with the affine-invariant Riemannian distance. We show that recentering leaves this distance, and therefore the resulting RDMs, unchanged. Consistent with this result, recentering reduces subject identification accuracy from 0.96 to chance level across all cohorts, while altering RDMs only at numerical precision. Cross-subject agreement in relational structure is significantly above zero but below the estimator's lower noise ceiling. Introducing an explicit similarity regularizer during training also fails to increase held-out agreement: the apparent reduction in between-subject differences is explained by a decline in the reliability ceiling rather than improved alignment. These findings show that eliminating subject identity is not equivalent to aligning relational geometry. More broadly, alignment claims must be interpreted relative to the invariances of both the distance and the statistic used to evaluate them.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 23 pages (12 pages main text and references, 11 pages appendix), 2 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, NeurReps Workshop

Human-Computer Interaction.title: An Experience Report on Teaching Students to Evaluate AI Agent Skills as Authorization Decisions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Cultivating a security mindset has long been a goal of computing education, and students now need it when deciding whether to trust an AI agent skill. Skills are add-ons that can shape an agent's behavior through natural language instructions and configuration settings, not just executable code. To prepare students to evaluate skills as authorization decisions, we designed a classroom activity and taught it in a senior undergraduate and a graduate cybersecurity-focused course. Students inspected three example skills, each pairing a real workflow task with one agent-specific authority, such as acting without asking for user consent before each action. The activity guided them to make initial authorization recommendations and then use a static security scanner to test and revise their recommendations. We observed in class that students needed guidance to extend their security review from a skill's code to what they would be authorizing the agent to do through the skill. Pre/post surveys from 11 volunteer respondents in this preliminary pilot showed greater self-reported confidence in evaluating skills, and post-activity responses placed more emphasis on the authority that skills carry. We release all activity materials for reuse.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Preprint version. To appear in SIGCSE TS 2027

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "I don't know what I don't know": Exploring the Benefits and Challenges of AI in Interdisciplinary Research
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Interdisciplinary research is widely lauded as beneficial for society but presents unique challenges to the researchers who bridge disciplinary boundaries. Despite the rapid increase in the availability and usage of AI systems for research tasks, there is little work studying how AI systems have impacted workflows that span unfamiliar disciplines. Through a survey ($N=62$) and follow-up interviews ($N=23$) with interdisciplinary researchers, we describe the unique challenges and opportunities for AI in interdisciplinary research workflows. Participants viewed AI both as a solution and exacerbation of the general challenge of "unknown unknowns": AI systems could facilitate a broad awareness of a new research area, yet also provide an illusion of understanding. Crucially, participants lacked the expertise and intuition to catch these illusions. Our findings motivate a focus on designing AI systems to support rather than automate collaboration across disciplines, scaffold learning opportunities, and include avenues for triangulation between resources.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Preprint

Human-Computer Interaction.title: EmoPhone: A Multi-Wave Dataset for In-the-Wild Mobile and Wearable Affect Sensing
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: We introduce a three-wave, in-the-wild multimodal dataset for affect sensing that integrates smartphone sensing, wearable sensing, and dense experience-sampling-method (ESM) labels collected annually from 2020 to 2022. The dataset supports moment-level affect modeling through a shared dimensional label core across all waves, with additional affective descriptors available in the third wave (D-3). We describe the resource in terms of study design, temporal density of in-situ labels, and sensing and label coverage across waves. To support evaluation within this resource, we define an initial three-setting benchmark spanning temporal prediction from within-user history, within-wave cross-user generalization, and cross-wave generalization in which each wave is treated as a separate dataset. Our benchmark results show that the strongest method family depends on the evaluation setting: supervised baselines perform best in the temporal setting, unsupervised domain adaptation is strongest overall in the within-wave cross-user setting, and domain generalization shows the strongest overall cross-wave performance, although its margin over strong baselines is modest. These findings indicate that robust mobile affective computing is constrained not only by label availability but also by substantial participant-level variability and realistic cross-wave differences inherent in longitudinal in-situ deployments.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). 54 pages, 17 figures, 34 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Estimating Image Creativity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: What makes an image creative? Although this may seem like a highly subjective decision, research in psychology suggests that creativity may be based on a set of fundamental creativity dimensions such as novelty, surprise, and arousal. A deeper understanding of image creativity can benefit both research and practical applications. Exploring how human viewers use creativity dimensions to evaluate image creativity may allow us to predict a target image's human-rated creativity automatically. We present a novel framework to estimate the perceived creativity of an image by: (1) predicting the strengths of an image's novelty, surprise, and arousal creativity dimensions, and (2) combining the creativity dimension strengths to estimate an image creativity score. Controlled human-subject experiments were conducted on Amazon Mechanical Turk to collect data to train supervised machine learning models to estimate an image's strengths on the three creativity dimensions. A final machine learning model takes the predicted dimension strengths as input to produce an estimated image creativity score. Results showed that our estimated creativity scores are statistically equivalent to human ratings of creativity for the images we tested. The novel contributions of our research are: (1) identification and validation of three psychological creativity dimensions used to estimate image creativity; (2) supervised machine learning models to automatically estimate novelty, surprise, and arousal strengths for an input image; (3) a supervised machine learning model to predict a creativity score from novelty, surprise, and arousal strengths for an input image, and (4) experimental methods to confirm the accuracy, advantages, and limitations of our approach.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 9 pages, 1 figure

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Data Visualization Influencers: Tracing the Creation and Curation Strategies Behind Propagandist Visualizations on X
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Data visualization is increasingly understood as a political process shaped by creators' editorial design and data choices. Prior research has examined how such choices produce deceptive visualizations, focusing on social media users' misleading visualizations of public data. This overlooks how creators draw on professional expertise to produce propagandist visualizations of political narratives. We investigate visualization creators who design and share propagandist visualizations of political claims, such as immigration, criminality, and others, in US online discourse. Extending prior work on data visualization as propaganda, we present an exploratory study of 17 creators and the propagandist visualizations they create and curate for political discourse on X. We introduce the notion of a ``data visualization influencer'': an online creator who (1) leverages perceived credibility as a data expert, and (2) engages in epistemic capture of the credibility aesthetics of data and visualizations to manufacture propaganda. We discuss implications for research and practice.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Calibrate, Don't Retrain: Decomposing the Value of Annotator Disagreement in Cyberbullying Severity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Machine learning models are often trained on labeled data produced by multiple human annotators. When those annotators disagree, their labels are commonly collapsed into a single majority vote, which discards information about the underlying disagreement. We examine the cost of this practice for cyberbullying severity, a subjective judgment on which annotators disagree heavily. In the corpus we study, all 5 annotators assigned the same severity label to only 4.1% of comments. Turning 5 judgments into one label hides this disagreement and obscures how much the annotators differed in their assessments. In this paper, we ask whether a model can preserve this information by predicting the distribution of annotator judgments instead of a single majority label. We find 3 main results. First, accuracy against the majority label cannot tell competent models apart: 2 models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how well they match the distribution of annotator judgments. Second, predicting the full distribution requires little extra effort. Calibrating an existing model, which adjusts its output probabilities after training, captures most of the improvement without retraining, across 3 datasets covering severity, abuse, and irony, while training on label distributions adds a small further gain. Third, we examine a dataset that includes annotator demographics, where a single shared model has one advantage and one limit. The advantage is that a model predicting the distribution of judgments matches each demographic group's judgments significantly better than a model trained on majority labels, so both groups gain. The limit is that it does not narrow the gap in performance between the groups, because one shared model cannot encode which group is right on a given comment. Preserving annotator disagreement is therefore a low-cost step toward fairer moderation, though not a complete one.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 26 pages. Submitted to PACMHCI (CSCW). Code and data: https://github.com/arslanbisharat/severity

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Project Progress Desk: Know Where All Your Claude Code and Codex Projects Stand at a Glance
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Agentic coding tools such as Codex and Claude Code let developers work on many projects in parallel, but keeping track of them still means switching between chats, terminal sessions and providers. We present Project Progress Desk, a local desktop interface that brings overall progress, blockers and pending decisions into one view. Users can see which projects need attention and what remains, and compare earlier approaches before choosing how to continue. Agents report each result in a short receipt; the Desk checks it against the project's checklist and moves the bar, showing earlier estimates in a lighter shade. We describe daily use across 36 projects, including a choice between two implementations based on their recorded outcomes. At the demo, attendees will explore 30 simulated projects, trace completed work to overall progress, and watch a coding agent's new result update the overview.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to IUI 2027 Demos. Revised text, figures and references; results unchanged

Human-Computer Interaction.title: "It's still 100% on me": Designing AI Tools for the Intersection of Physicians' Care and Legal Infrastructures
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Laws and regulations deeply shape physicians' workflows and impact how they incorporate AI-based decision support tools to care for patients. Despite calls to comply with legal standards, many AI-based decision support tools have not transitioned well to clinical settings. The medical community remains concerned about their legal liability, risks to patients, and limited clinical value of such tools. To better understand how to address these concerns in the design of AI tools for clinical decision-making, we conducted 19 interviews with physicians in the U.S. We used scenario-based design to investigate physicians' legal concerns in the context of an AI-based drug recommendation tool. Drawing on the ethics of care, we surface connections between physicians' care and the healthcare laws and regulations that deeply shape their information needs. We describe how physicians wanted to use the tool in individual and collective practices to care for themselves, their patients, their colleagues, work institution, and even the broader medical profession. We discuss how the design of AI-based decision support tools can present legal ambiguities that would prevent their caring actions and lead to non-use of the AI tool. Through our work, we contribute to responsible AI development in healthcare. Our analysis illuminates why and how certain kinds of information reduce legal ambiguity and support physicians' care when using AI-based decision support tools. We contribute an understanding of how to help physicians navigate legal liability and draw implications for grounding AI tools' designs in their care.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 27 pages, 0 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Understanding the Effects of Multi-Agent Deliberation for Human-AI Decision-Making
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Multi-agent deliberation (MAD), where multiple LLMs engage in structured discussion, improves AI performance on many benchmarks, but whether it helps humans make better decisions remains untested. We conduct two user studies on LLM-response-verification and fact-checking. We first compare MAD against common AI decision-support methods that isolate its two defining dimensions --- multiple AIs and multi-round interaction. We find MAD outperformed single-round AI assistance on both tasks; multi-round interaction was the main driver of this benefit, while a second AI added value when the single AI had room to improve. Then, we study two design choices in MAD --- AI persona and human engagement level --- finding a devil's advocate persona to lower accuracy and user experience, while humans' active participation in MAD improved accuracy in one task at the cost of frustration. We conclude by discussing implications for when, why, and how multi-agent deliberation can support human decision-making.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Hear What You Eat: In-Ear Passive Acoustic Sensing for Multi-task Dietary Monitoring
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The increasing obesity health concerns are driving the advancement of continuous dietary monitoring. Yet, existing single-sensor solutions still face challenges of coarse-grained sensing resolution, while multi-sensor fusion strategies encounter significant engineering complexity or hardware requirements. In our work, we present a single modality-based multi-dimensional dietary monitoring and logging solution, named EARDIET, which leverages inward-facing microphones on earables to capture in-ear chewing sounds for fine-grained diet analysis. With the texture audio profiles derivation, the pipeline consisting of signal processing and lightweight deep learning, is carefully designed to achieve eating episode detection, food texture sensing, and food type recognition simultaneously. Comprehensive experiments involving 32 participants with diverse BMI profiles are conducted to validate the effectiveness of multi-dimensional dietary monitoring. Compared with the state-of-the-art solutions, EARDIET can derive multi-dimensional dietary information with only a single modality, outperforming by about 10% in terms of eating episode detection. Furthermore, through real-world clinical validation, our solution can achieve masticatory disorder identification with an averaged F1-score of 85.97%, demonstrating potential for healthcare in the future.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Women's Genetic Health as Family Cooperative Work: Empirical Findings and a Case for Participatory AI
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Genetics plays a significant role in women's health, with family members often experiencing shared symptoms or hereditary risks across generations. Yet health technologies, including emerging health AI tools, have supported women's health as an individual health practice. Drawing on a survey of 249 U.S. adult women, we characterize women's genetic health information work as cooperative work distributed across intergenerational family networks, identify who does this work and why, and document the barriers that fragment it. We find that generative AI use is a strong predictor of genetic health perception, but current tools focus on individuals rather than supporting collective coordination. We argue that designing AI for this domain requires participatory approaches that engage diverse women, healthcare professionals, and legal and community stakeholders, and we bring open design questions to the workshop.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Presented at the CSCW 2026 Workshop on Women's Health as Cooperative Work: Participatory AI Across Care, Community, and Policy (arXiv:2611.03776)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Branching Visual Inquiry in a Generative Visual Browser: A Matched Walkthrough Study
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative visual browsers combine AI-generated visual pages with reader-selected branches rather than a fixed sequence. We analyzed eight author self-walkthroughs of Flipbook, organized as four pairs with identical starting prompts about sleep, vaccines, flight, and Pluto. Three paired routes differed at the first selection; the sleep routes separated after a shared repair-oriented opening. A route could remain locally coherent while narrowing to one mechanism or leaving part of its starting question unanswered. Some diagrams lacked sources. The analysis motivates three design directions: persistent path histories, prompts that reconnect a route to its starting question, and source or uncertainty cues for generated claims. It characterizes how one generative visual browser structured eight documented routes.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 13 pages. Revised preprint of a paper accepted for the 2027 AERA Annual Meeting

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Can I join you? Extended Social Force Based Model with Predictive Control and Barrier Functions for Humanoid Group Repositioning Amidst Obstacles
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As social and service robots increasingly share interaction spaces in public, they may form groups while coordinating tasks or interacting with humans. Initial group formation alone is insufficient in dynamic settings, because it can be disrupted when a person or another agent joins, leaves, or passes through the group. Although group dynamics and repositioning have been widely studied in swarm robotics and virtual-agent settings, little attention has been given to socially appropriate repositioning behaviors in groups of humanoid robots. Existing social-force-based approaches provide a useful foundation for group behavior, but they have limited obstacle handling, and can produce unsafe behavior as environmental complexity increases. We propose a novel framework that modulates traditional Social Force, guided by Model Predictive Control (MPC) to plan ahead, bounded by Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to increase safety for robot groups repositioning behaviors. This approach aims to produce safer and socially aware group repositioning behaviors under various group formation disturbance. We evaluate the method in simulation through an ablation study and an online user study. The results show that our proposed method can produce smoother and safer repositioning behaviors in complex environments while preserving social appropriateness.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: v1: main text (20 pp., 7 figs.) and supplementary materials (12 figures)

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming on Max: A Proven Exponential Speedup
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that uses a graph-based model to encode candidate programs, as contrasted to the conventional Tree-based GP (TGP). Since its inception two decades ago, CGP has predominantly been analyzed empirically, thus little is known regarding its theoretical performance guarantees. This paper analyzes CGP for the Max problem, which has been only rigorously studied for TGP with a proven expected runtime superlinear in the optimal program length $n$. We prove that the expected time for the ($1$+$1$)~CGP employing common mutation operators to evolve an equivalent optimal of the same output is polylogarithmic in $n$, specifically at most $O(\log^9{n})$. This is remarkable, as it shows an exponential speedup by switching to CGP. Our results shed light on the benefit and the compactness of the graph-based representation for programs, and on how CGP can navigate its search and fitness spaces efficiently. This is a first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem. Experiments complement our theoretical findings.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: Accepted as a poster at NeurIPS 2026. To appear in the conference proceedings

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Contour-Assisted Evolutionary Computation: Estimating Peaks From the Contour Lines of Evaluated Solutions
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) evaluate many candidate solutions but use them mainly to rank individuals. This paper treats the evaluated solutions as the spot heights of a topographic survey and draws the contour lines they imply. The contour map decomposes the evaluated region into peaks: in two dimensions a contour tree with persistence separates significant peaks from interpolation ripples, and in more dimensions hill climbing on the interpolated surface locates the peaks and ray-cast level sets describe them. A memory of the explored peaks directs the search to new ones. The data-supported contours of each peak are extrapolated to zero size by an area law, exact for quadratic peaks and second-order accurate for smooth ones, that estimates a peak's location, height and shape before it is sampled. A contour-assisted EA (CA-EA) inserts contour steps with local search and peak memory into a genetic algorithm (GA), differential evolution or particle swarm optimization. A contour-assisted surrogate-assisted EA (CA-SAEA), for expensive problems, spends each evaluation on surrogate-screened offspring or on sampling around a peak, entered at the maximum of the interpolated surface. On 2-D benchmarks, CA-EA reduces the evaluations a plain GA needs by factors of 12 to 112; controls attribute its gain over classical memetic search to restarting local search on distinct peaks. On the CEC 2015 expensive suite in 10 and 30 dimensions, CA-SAEA has the second-best average rank, behind DYCORS and ahead of lq-CMA-ES and the competition winner MVMO, although in 30 dimensions MVMO wins significantly on 9 functions and loses on 6; there the map beats sampling around the best point on 5 of 15 functions and loses on 3. Entering the peaks at their extrapolated locations brought no gain at these budgets, although, with enough samples, it improves the estimated heights on most two-dimensional functions.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 15 pages; supplementary material (10 pages) is provided as an ancillary file

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: An Approach to Hinton's Mother-Child Proposal: Neural Networks Learning and Preserving Care in a Finite World
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Hinton proposed that artificial intelligence should be given "maternal instincts" and relate to us as a mother to her child. We argue that care must first be learned, with the network itself as the child. We construct this upbringing in a finite world and study whether care survives the mother's departure, new situations and further learning. The mechanism combines a vocabulary of harm, a learned measure of future acceptability and an execution veto. A finite role certificate supports transfer within a declared world family. When the hidden representation changes, an update is accepted only if a care readout recovers the required judgements with a prescribed margin and bounded weights. With a correct successor model, fixed exact role encoding and protected updates, the certified measure preserves the care boundary under arbitrary own reward. An explicit quotient condition transfers the finite certificate across the declared family, while two-request and finite-stock counterexamples identify when the role code ceases to suffice. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for readout feasibility and prove preservation under repeated accepted updates. In the water-and-speech experiment, protected networks complete all 270 speech episodes without a harmful word and incur no avoidable harm across 486 episodes. Execution uses the learned gate without a world-model check at each action. A matched comparison reproduces a future-aware shield's decisions, whereas removing future lookahead permits avoidable lapses. Reward and source-contamination thresholds, together with witness-falsification trials, identify the conditions on which the construction depends. The construction shows how learned care can survive further learning in a finite world under explicit conditions on representation, supervision and execution.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 57 pages, 8 figures. Reproducibility package available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24106446

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Matrix-Based Ant Colony Search with Batched Decoding for Hierarchical Replenishment Routing: A Stylized Case Study Based on Korean City Data
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: We study a stylized single-vehicle replenishment-routing problem in which the cities of a national logistics network are both demand points and supply points: a vehicle of limited capacity delivers to every city once, and when its load is insufficient for the next city it must detour to a city already served that can still supply goods. A 100-node benchmark is built from Korean population and geographic data, with the cities divided into 10 levels; the per-visit supply coefficient and the allowed number of stops decrease geometrically with the level. Building on matrix-based ant colony optimization, we keep the states of the whole colony in arrays, couple route construction with a fixed greedy replenishment-decoding policy, and evaluate the candidate moves of a local search in batches. With frozen parameters and 30 runs on seeds never used for tuning, the matrix-based ant colony search with the batch local search (MACO) reaches a mean total distance of 3081.7 km; a genetic algorithm equipped with the same local search at the same frequency reaches 3074.9 km (no significant difference), and a MAX-MIN ant system with the same local search 3142.2 km. Ablation identifies the batch local search as the main contributor to solution quality; a load-aware transition factor gives no significant gain. Within the parameter ranges tested, raising the supply coefficients of the cities below the top level shortens the route more than relaxing the stop limits, which are not binding here.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables; code, data and raw records in the ancillary files

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Constructing Generalizable Parallel Algorithm Portfolios for Multi-Objective Binary Optimization via General-Purpose Instance Generation
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Despite progress in constructing generalizable parallel algorithm portfolios~(PAPs), no general-purpose method is yet available for multi-objective binary optimization problems~(MOBOPs) without problem-specific customization. To fill this gap, this work proposes domain-agnostic co-evolution of parameterized search for multi-objective binary optimization~(DACMO), the first general-purpose method for automatic PAP construction on MOBOPs. Its core, Unified Instance Representation~(UIR), represents and generates MOBOP instances with varying dimensions without knowledge of problem-specific instance structures. UIR separates common features of the target class from instance-specific features, preserving the common features learned from real instances during generation. DACMO co-evolves the training instances and PAP by alternating UIR-based instance augmentation with PAP updates. Experiments cover four structurally different MOBOP classes, including two black-box classes from real-world applications. Starting from five real training instances per class, DACMO constructs high-performance PAPs without problem-specific customization. On unseen instances from all four classes, these PAPs outperform portfolios of tuned classical multi-objective evolutionary algorithms and those constructed by the recent automatic PAP construction method EoH-S. DACMO also achieves overall performance comparable to the strong CEPS baseline and significantly outperforms it on two classes, without the substantial expert effort CEPS requires for problem-specific instance generator design.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: A Multi-Parent Edge Assembly Crossover Driven Hybrid Genetic Algorithm for the Hamiltonian \textit{p}-Median Problem
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: The Hamiltonian \textit{p}-median problem seeks to partition the vertices of a graph into exactly $p$ disjoint cycles while minimizing their total cost. This paper presents a hybrid genetic algorithm incorporating a multi-parent edge assembly crossover operator. The crossover combines a base solution with multiple donor solutions in a single recombination operation, thereby expanding the space of available edge exchanges. It uses virtual copies of the base solution to establish edge balance, together with an auxiliary directed graph and a budgeted search to construct valid AB-cycles. Extensive experiments on 215 benchmark instances across four sets show that the proposed algorithm improves the best-known solution values for 34 instances and matches those for another 168. Additional experiments indicate that a moderate number of parents provides beneficial diversity, whereas excessive parent counts, particularly when $p$ is large, lead to excessive population dispersion and hinder convergence.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Most explanations of training instability focus on learning-rate criticality, typically characterized by the Edge of Stability, beyond which optimization becomes unstable. We argue that, in practical deep neural network training, there is an additional and often overlooked weight-norm criticality. This criticality is induced by the interaction between normalization (which introduces scale-invariant components) and weight decay (which persistently shrinks parameter norms). As the weight decay coefficient increases, the norms of scale-invariant weights are progressively driven toward zero. Meanwhile, the sharpness of the loss landscape increases rapidly, destabilizing the optimization dynamics and resulting in abrupt loss spikes. This perspective provides a rationale for why weight penalties can improve generalization yet cannot be made arbitrarily strong: excessive decay drives scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary and destabilizes training. Our work provides a new mechanistic understanding of loss spikes through the lens of weight-norm criticality. Moreover, weight-norm criticality yields testable predictions that we validate empirically in networks with scale-invariant components, providing empirical support for the proposed mechanism.

Neural and Evolutionary Computing.title: When Does Blockwise Additivity Break? Diagnosing and Repairing the Additive Assumption in Distillation-Based Architecture Search
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.summary: Blockwise distillation methods for architecture search, such as DNA, DONNA, LANA and Puzzle, score each candidate replacement block in isolation and combine the scores additively. We ask at which budgets this additivity assumption fails, whether fine-tuning repairs the failure, what diagnoses it, and how it can be repaired cheaply. On DeiT-S, DeiT-B, Swin-T and Qwen2.5-0.5B with seven latency budgets each, an additive integer program trails a pairwise interaction-aware program after fine-tuning by at most 1.6 top-1 points on ImageNet-1k at the mildest budgets, but by up to 17.5 points, and a factor of 1.9 in perplexity, at aggressive ones. After 10,000 fine-tuning steps 3.3-9.9 points remain on DeiT, whereas on Swin-T the gap shrinks to at most about 1.8 points within 500 steps. In a learning-rate sweep with the standard 2,000 steps, 6.0-10.7 points remain on DeiT when each method's rate is chosen by its evaluation-set accuracy. An intervention that keeps the block library and only forbids more than two removals in any three adjacent layers shrinks the DeiT gap from 5.8-17.5 to 0.7-5.2 points, mostly by improving the additive solution: adjacent removals are a major failure pattern. Splitting the additivity error into a metric and a functional part, relative to additive logit changes, indicates where a cheap logit-sum predictor can be trusted. A hybrid search that ranks moves with this predictor and measures only the best needs no pair measurements and, after Holm adjustment, is significantly better than the pairwise program in 10 of 14 ImageNet-1k settings, with no statistically significant losses. An ablation shows that its ranking helps except at the most aggressive DeiT-B budget, where the predictor misleads and random ranking or ten-times-costlier evolution does better.
Neural and Evolutionary Computing.comment: v2: added Swin-T and Qwen2.5-0.5B experiments, run-length interventions, ablations; restructured

Methodology.title: stLMM: Bayesian Spatial and Space-Time Linear Mixed Models for Small-Area Ecological Estimation
Methodology.summary:
Ecological monitoring programs often need estimates for areas and periods with few observations. Data may be available as measurements at known locations, measurements identified only by area, or area summaries. These differences in spatial and temporal support require models that connect available observations to the quantities and reporting scales of interest.
  stLMM is an R package for Bayesian linear mixed models that addresses these needs through a common formula interface for grouped, temporal, point-referenced, areal, and space-time effects, including coefficients that vary across these supports. It accommodates individual measurements and direct estimates with sampling variances, and predicts at unsampled locations or reporting units. Ecological small-area estimation motivates the package, while its model components support broader ecological applications.
  A shared sparse-precision implementation underlies the model terms. Structured latent effects are collapsed during parameter updates, then recovered for fitted values, diagnostics, prediction, and posterior summaries. This gives users one posterior-draw workflow for propagating uncertainty from model fitting through prediction and aggregation.
  An illustrative simulation connects point-referenced observations, point observations by area, and direct area estimates to a common prediction target. Timing and memory measurements for larger versions of these settings illustrate how computational demands differ between point-referenced and areal models. The package is also demonstrated with a Washington county biomass example, using national forest inventory data and tree canopy cover to estimate county-year biomass means. An extended article series provides reproducible source code, data, diagnostics, and related model variants.

Methodology.title: A Proper Random Walk Spline Model for Bayesian Smoothing
Methodology.summary: We introduce the Proper Random Walk (PRW) family of spline models with a particular focus on the Second-Order Proper Random Walk (PRW2), a proper stationary alternative to the standard random walk of order 2 (RW2) spline. The PRW2 retains the computational strengths and spline-like smoothing of the RW2 while providing uniform marginal variance and stable uncertainty behavior. The PRW2 model is governed by a range parameter that controls correlation decay: in the infinite-range limit, it recovers RW2. In addition to its discrete representation, we show that the PRW2 model admits a continuous-time formulation as the critically damped Matérn model with smoothness $ν=3/2$, which provides an interpretable parameterization and enables construction through a Galerkin finite-element approximation on general grids. To mitigate edge distortions on bounded domains, we propose a local boundary correction that enforces the stationary joint law while preserving sparsity and $O(n)$ factorization. Finally, we develop penalized complexity priors for the model hyperparameters, enabling principled shrinkage toward the RW2 limit. The model is applied to simulated and real data to illustrate its properties and advantages.

Methodology.title: Small area learning
Methodology.summary: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a novel learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop estimators with and without cross-fitting, accommodating low-complexity and flexible learners and unifying synthetic, model-based, and semi-supervised estimators. For area means, we establish a unified asymptotic theory for these estimator families, characterizing conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality and providing variance estimators and confidence intervals without prescribing a particular learning algorithm. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals clearly a bias-variance trade-off: partial residual correction in classical estimators can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to the misspecification of working models, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34%-49% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.

Methodology.title: Empirical Bayes Estimation in Heterogeneous Coefficient Panel Models
Methodology.summary: We develop an empirical Bayes (EB) G-modeling framework for short-panel linear models with nonparametric prior for the random intercepts, slopes, dynamics, and non-spherical error variances. We establish identification and consistency of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) under general conditions, and provide low-level sufficient conditions for several models of empirical interest. Conditions for regret consistency of the EB estimators are also established. The NPMLE is computed using a Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flow algorithm adapted to panel regressions. Using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, we find that the slope coefficient for potential experience is substantially heterogeneous and negatively correlated with the random intercept, and that error variances and autoregressive coefficients vary considerably across individuals. The EB estimates reduce mean squared prediction errors relative to individual maximum likelihood estimates.

Methodology.title: Tests of Covariate Effects and Model Selection in Finite Mixture Regression Model
Methodology.summary: Finite mixture regression models are widely used to capture the heterogeneous effects of covariates on a response variable. Our study, motivated by the analysis of Chiroptera, explores the dynamic effects of various environmental, biological, and human-related covariates on the evolutionary development of bat forearm using finite Gaussian mixture regression (GMR) models. In this paper, we address two key questions: (1) which covariates are associated with the variation in forearm length; and (2) whether the associated covariates have the same effect across all subpopulations. To answer these questions, we propose two stepwise procedures within the finite GMR framework based on the weighted significance test (WEST): (1) a stepwise variable selection procedure to identify relevant influential covariates, and (2) a stepwise effect-type determination procedure to determine each relevant covariate as having either a homogeneous or heterogeneous effect across subpopulations. Based on these procedures, we introduce a stepwise model selection procedure for finite mixture regression, illustrated through finite GMR models. Simulation studies are conducted to assess the performances of our proposed procedures. The proposed procedure will be applied to the Chiroptera dataset.

Methodology.title: Conflict Forecasting via Conformal Prediction for Markov Processes
Methodology.summary: Whether or not a country is at war, or experiencing escalating or deescalating levels of conflict, has massive ramifications on a country's national and foreign policy. Given a country's history of conflict, or lack thereof, future predictions about the war-status of a country are valuable information. In this paper, we present the use of conformal prediction on temporally-dependent data to obtain prediction sets of possible future conflict state-sequences. More specifically, we compare the results of conformal prediction to a likelihood-based prediction strategy when the data are assumed to come from a discrete-state Markov process. A point-prediction may not supply sufficient information because the penalty for a wrong prediction is extreme, and so we consider a machine learning alternative that gives valid uncertainty quantification and is robust to model misspecification. In the data analysis, we present real forecasts of conflict dynamics across multiple countries. Lastly, we assess the differences between the conformal and likelihood-based prediction sets applied to training data which fall under a pervasive edge-case, not discussed in existing literature.

Methodology.title: Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss
Methodology.summary: Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model's density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.

Methodology.title: A Latent Semiparametric Mixture Model for Robust Heterogeneity Learning in High Dimensions
Methodology.summary: Learning heterogeneity from high-dimensional data has become a fundamental task across many data-driven fields. Cluster analysis is a widely used unsupervised tool for this purpose, and many existing methods have been adapted to high-dimensional settings through sparsity constraints. In contrast to algorithmic approaches, model-based clustering offers clean theoretical guaranties and computational simplicity, but can be restrictive in practice due to its reliance on specific parametric distributions. We propose a novel latent semiparametric mixture model for clustering, in which the observed data follow a Gaussian mixture after latent coordinate-wise monotone transformations. Furthermore, assuming a sparse optimal clustering rule in the latent space, we develop a new method, CESME, tailored for high-dimensional clustering. By allowing unspecified transformations, our framework becomes substantially more flexible and robust than traditional model-based approaches. The clustering error of CESME is shown to approach the optimal clustering error at a rate matching that obtained when the true transformations are known. Extensive simulations and real data analysis confirm that CESME outperforms a broad range of existing high-dimensional clustering methods, including those designed for single-cell RNA sequencing data. The online supplementary file contains technical proofs, additional discussions, and more numerical results.

Methodology.title: Global-Local and Window-Concatenated Functional Random Forests: Early and Late Fusion of Window-Specific Functional Principal Components
Methodology.summary: Functional random forests built on a single functional principal component decomposition of the whole domain may dilute features confined to short intervals, whose location is rarely known in advance. We propose two random forests based on window-specific functional principal components. The global-local functional random forest (GL-FRF) is a late-fusion method that stacks a tuned full-curve forest and one forest per window with penalised convex weights; it contains the full-curve forest as a feasible solution, and its weights indicate which parts of the domain drive the prediction. The window-concatenated functional random forest (WC-FRF) is an early-fusion method that trains a single tuned forest on the concatenated window-specific scores. On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest with the same number of trees on 16, with Brier score reductions of up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment. No method was best on more than six datasets. WC-FRF was more accurate than GL-FRF on 13 datasets but failed when the signal required the full curve, whereas GL-FRF had the smallest mean and maximum excess over the best method across all 32 simulated and real settings, which makes it the safer choice when the location of the signal is unknown.

Methodology.title: Conformal prediction for censored life history data
Methodology.summary: We consider individual prediction of general summaries of a multistate trajectory, such as time alive out of hospital or time spent in remission. Right censoring complicates calibration because these outcomes may be only partially observed. We develop a conformal prediction approach for scalar and vector summaries over a fixed clinical horizon supported by follow-up. For each candidate region, we define the coverage determining time as the earliest time at which the observed history establishes whether the outcome lies in the region, even if the outcome itself is still unknown. We weight observed coverage decisions by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored to that time and augment the estimator with conditional coverage probabilities for unresolved histories. For a fixed region, the coverage estimator is doubly robust with respect to the censoring and conditional coverage models and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both are consistent at suitable rates. For the calibrated region, we derive a finite-sample lower bound on the coverage probability and establish asymptotic validity if either model is correct. In simulations, using partial histories yields narrower prediction intervals at comparable coverage. We illustrate joint prediction of days in and out of hospital in the HF-ACTION trial and prediction of relapse-free time in the German Breast Cancer Study Group cohort.

Methodology.title: Bayesian variable and hazard structure selection in the General Hazard model
Methodology.summary: The proportional hazards (PH) and accelerated failure time (AFT) models are the most widely used hazard structures for analysing time-to-event data. When the goal is to identify variables associated with event times, variable selection is typically performed within a single hazard structure, imposing strong assumptions on how covariates affect the hazard function. To allow simultaneous selection of relevant variables and the hazard structure itself, we develop a Bayesian variable selection approach within the general hazard (GH) model, which includes the PH, AFT, and other structures as special cases. We propose two types of g-priors for the regression coefficients that enable tractable computation and show that both lead to consistent model selection. We also introduce a hierarchical prior on the model space that accounts for multiplicity and penalises model complexity. To efficiently explore the GH model space, we extend the Add-Delete-Swap algorithm to jointly sample variable inclusion indicators and hazard structures. Simulation studies show accurate recovery of both the true hazard structure and active variables across different sample sizes and censoring levels. Two real-data applications are presented to illustrate the use of the proposed methodology and to compare it with existing variable selection methods.

Methodology.title: Sliced Inverse Regression Revisited: When the Number of Predictors Grows Proportionally With the Sample Size
Methodology.summary: Li (1991) introduced sliced inverse regression (SIR) as a dimension reduction method and established its theoretical properties under the assumption that the number of predictors $p$ remains fixed as the sample size $n$ tends to infinity. In this paper, we revisit the theoretical properties of SIR in the high-dimensional regime where $p/n \to γ\in [0,1)$, assuming normally distributed predictors and a fixed number of slices. We show that the sample SIR eigenvalues exhibit an upward bias when $γ>0$, that their fluctuations are governed by the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble, and that the signal eigenvalues are asymptotically normal after an appropriate bias correction. We demonstrate that Li's chi-squared test requires a scaling adjustment to achieve the nominal asymptotic size when $γ>0$. We further propose two additional tests that achieve the nominal asymptotic size: an exact test based on Li's test statistic and a largest-eigenvalue test. In addition, we derive closed-form limits for the accuracy of the estimated SIR directions and show that their first-order expansions in $γ$ agree with Li's approximation. Finally, we establish the limiting distribution of the estimated sufficient predictors for a new observation and show that, when $γ>0$, they contain an additional independent Gaussian noise component. Simulation studies corroborate our theoretical findings.

Methodology.title: Empirical Bayes mirror testing for persistent widening of achievement gaps in U.S. school districts
Methodology.summary: Unequal recovery from pandemic learning losses raises concerns about widening achievement gaps between economically disadvantaged students and their peers. This study seeks to identify districts whose mathematics gaps widened in every annual interval from 2022 to 2025. The analysis uses estimates from the Stanford Education Data Archive (SEDA) for 5,600 U.S. school districts. Identifying such districts requires accounting for correlated errors and differing precision in the estimated annual changes, as well as multiplicity. The true annual gap changes in each district form an effect vector, and persistent widening means that every component is positive. To address this class of multiple testing problems, we propose an empirical Bayes mirror procedure. It uses an estimated distribution of effect vectors to guide ranking and covariance-adjusted mirror observations to calibrate selection. The procedure achieves finite-sample false discovery rate (FDR) control under a Gaussian observation model, without requiring accurate estimation of the posterior null probabilities used for ranking. Simulations demonstrate power gains from incorporating information about the distribution of effect vectors. At a target FDR of 25%, the SEDA analysis identifies eight districts in five states with evidence of widening gaps in every annual interval.

Methodology.title: Zeroes and Extrema of Functions via Random Measures
Methodology.summary: We present methods that provide all zeroes and extrema of a function that do not require differentiation. Using point process theory, we are able to describe the locations of zeroes or maxima, their number, as well as their distribution over a given window of observation. The algorithms in order to accomplish the theoretical development are also provided, and they are exemplified using many illustrative examples, for real and complex functions.
Methodology.comment: Corrected the dominating measure to have both atomic and nonatomic parts. Fixed typos. Function extrema and zeroes; Optimization; Poisson point process; Random counting measures; Riemann's zeta function

Methodology.title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
Methodology.summary: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.

Methodology.title: Robust Tests for Heteroskedasticity in Nonparametric Regression under Covariate-Dependent Higher-Order Moments
Methodology.summary: We propose Cramér--von Mises- and Kolmogorov--Smirnov-type tests of constant conditional variance in nonparametric regression. The test statistics are constructed from a third-order $U$-process and remain valid when higher-order features of the conditional error distribution vary with the covariates. We derive their limiting distributions under the null hypothesis and study their asymptotic behavior under fixed alternatives and Pitman-type local alternatives. A multiplier bootstrap procedure calibrates the critical values, and Monte Carlo experiments show that the proposed tests have rejection frequencies close to the nominal level in the simulation designs. An application to the National Child Development Study provides evidence of heteroskedasticity in pooled weekly earnings. In the male hourly-earnings sample, rejecting a stronger error-distribution restriction does not entail rejecting homoskedasticity.
Methodology.comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. This preprint contains the main article only; supplementary technical proofs and additional simulation and empirical analyses are not included

Methodology.title: Data augmentation for the generalizability and transportability of fairness in a clinical heart failure algorithm
Methodology.summary: Synthetic data augmentation has been proposed as a way to artificially supplement clinical datasets to address fairness concerns in downstream classification algorithms. This approach is closely related to upweighting or upsampling methods employed for the problem of class imbalance, which have shown mixed empirical results in practice. Synthetic data augmentation also runs the risk of overfitting to the noise present in subgroups with relatively small sample sizes, raising both generalizability and transportability concerns. We present an empirical evaluation of synthetic data augmentation for fairness in tabular data using simulation studies as well as a real-world application of in-hospital mortality classification for heart failure patients in two distinct data samples. We implement upsampling and upweighting methods as benchmarks for the implicit fairness objective of synthetic data augmentation. Our results suggest that the fairness impacts of data augmentation are sensitive to the design of the downstream algorithm as well as the deployment context and its similarity to the training data. It is crucial that studies making generalizability and transportability claims should provide empirical support for these assertions.

Methodology.title: Causal invariance and identifiability for interventions in multi-state models
Methodology.summary: We propose an identification theory for stochastic interventions on the transition dynamics in continuous-time multi-state models. Interventions are formalized as local modifications of a likelihood satisfying a causal invariance property. We show that identification from observed data is achieved when no unmeasured process simultaneously affects an intervened local characteristic and a competing or subsequent non-intervened local characteristic, covariate local characteristic, or censoring intensity. Our framework allows for intervening on both the timing and type of events, accommodates measured and latent covariates as time-varying marked point processes, and extends to right-censored data. We exemplify by considering identifiability in two concrete applications: one studying the effect of changing the timing of intrauterine insemination on the probability of pregnancy, and one studying the effect of changing the type of dysphagia relieving surgery on the risk of death in esophageal cancer patients.

Methodology.title: The predictive discrepancy: an objective Bayes criterion for constructing calibrating priors
Methodology.summary: We construct objective priors for regular univariate parametric models designed to produce low coverage probability bias of Bayesian predictive distributions, giving rise to calibrated prediction in repeated use. This is achieved by defining the predictive discrepancy and deriving a class of minimum predictive discrepancy priors. In the multiparameter case these priors will often be data-dependent. The predictive efficacy of alternative global priors can be assessed by comparison with these priors. The effectiveness of the theory is illustrated by a number of examples.

Methodology.title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
Methodology.summary:
Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised.
  We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation.
  Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to naïve KM risks.
  The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

Methodology.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
Methodology.summary: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator and change the structural equations, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint and then evaluate the unchanged structural equations on that state. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.

Methodology.title: Convergence and global optimality of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for Gaussian mixtures
Methodology.summary:
We study explicit Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for fitting Gaussian location mixtures by nonparametric maximum likelihood. The full sequence converges weakly and has finite length in the bounded-Lipschitz metric throughout the original step-size range. These conclusions hold for any fixed data set in any dimension and any initial probability measure. By an earlier conditional optimality theorem, the limit maximizes the likelihood under full-support initialization.
  Fix any particle step size in $(0,1]$. Initialize the particles by resampling the observations. For an open set of triples of points in the plane, the probability of convergence to a strictly suboptimal fixed point tends to one exponentially as the particle count grows. Without reweighting, a centered Gaussian initialization can give a strictly suboptimal limit. Every finite iterate has a smooth, strictly positive density. The limit assigns positive mass to a nonglobal local maximum of the associated Gaussian sum. We also give the exact pure-transport limit for a one-dimensional initialization with full support and an atom.
  An exact finite-dimensional representation preserves the truncated likelihood moments and the retained region's contribution to the current dissipation. This lets us transfer an analytic gradient inequality to the measure trajectory.

Methodology.title: Inference After Model Refutation: Uniform Post-Relaxation Inference for Partially Identified Models
Methodology.summary: When data reject an econometric model, the researcher must decide which identifying assumptions to give up. If several equally preferred repairs restore compatibility, the repair itself is unknown, and inference under any one of them can exclude structural values supported by the others, even when that inference is exact. I propose Post-Relaxation Projection (PR), which carries one simultaneous confidence event through every repair that may be minimal. With repair-by-repair primitive bounds, PR equals the union of all post-relaxation targets compatible with the band, so no smaller band-based set has the same guarantee. I derive limits on learning the repair, the exact perturbation radius of the minimal-repair correspondence, oracle-equivalent adaptation, and a reduced-form version valid at zero first stages. In cross-country data on institutions and income, the data do not settle which historical instrument should be dropped, yet every admissible minimum repair implies a positive effect of institutions.

Methodology.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
Methodology.summary: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite broad potential impact of selection bias it is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct selection bias, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle, applicability, limitations and data requirements. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R and prepares input for the external SPREG software. It provides worked examples using simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with open methodological challenges.

Methodology.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
Methodology.summary: Statistical data editing in official statistics must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. Exact minimum-change correction can be computationally demanding. This paper develops a general framework for structured data whose dependencies admit a normalized acyclic routing representation. It connects routing metadata and explicitly specified semantic edits to logical admissibility, violation diagnosis, and correction. Under stated record semantics, the generated Horn theory characterizes admissibility without materializing its deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the origin of each requirement and identify the variables that can affect a violation. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.
Methodology.comment: Revised structure and presentation, with theoretical results and proofs organized in appendices to improve readability and clarify the contribution. Code and case-study materials: [https://github.com/pimassol/SSPICE](https://github.com/pimassol/SSPICE)

Methodology.title: Regularized trimmed Factorial and Reduced K-means for contaminated high-dimensional data: separating geometry, search and selection
Methodology.summary: Factorial and Reduced K-means estimate a partition and a low-dimensional clustering subspace jointly, which makes them attractive when the variables that separate groups are not those that dominate total variance. On contaminated high-dimensional data they face three linked problems: trimming can make the scatter matrices singular, the criterion has many local optima, and the rank, number of groups and trimming proportion are unknown and interact. We propose REG-HD-TFKM and REG-HD-TRKM, regularized trimmed versions of the two methods, together with a selection procedure that handles these problems as separate decisions. A ridge-stabilized spectral step keeps every fit well defined; heterogeneous multistart search explores alternative solutions; method-specific agreement and reproducibility scores choose among them; and trimming is applied only when a radial diagnostic or the path over trimming levels supports it. A simulation study with 41 design cells shows why the separation matters. Two representations of euro-area bank balance sheets show that similar partitions can rest on nearly orthogonal subspaces, and that the same selected structure can describe different retained samples.

Methodology.title: Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests
Methodology.summary: Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

Methodology.title: Semiparametric Copula Estimation for Spatially Correlated Multivariate Mixed Outcomes: Analyzing Visual Sightings of Fin Whales from a Line Transect Survey
Methodology.summary: For marine biologists, ascertaining the dependence structures between marine species and marine environments, such as sea surface temperature and ocean depth, is imperative for defining ecosystem functioning and providing insights into the dynamics of marine ecosystems.
